blocks.heading: 🎨 BRIEF
blocks.text: A streaming service wants their new home screen critiqued before it ships. The client keeps saying it 'feels off' but can't tell me why. That's the job today — before you can fix a design, you have to be able to name exactly what's in it: line, shape, colour, texture and space. Pin those down and you can finally talk about what's actually wrong.
The elements of design: line, shape, space, texture, colour

items: Identify the five elements of design in a digital product.
Describe how each element is used.
Use correct terms, not general words like "nice" or "bright".

blocks.title: Spotting the five elements
blocks.brief: A short clip pausing on a streaming app screen and naming where line, shape, space, texture and colour are used. Suggested source: a teacher-filmed annotated screen recording of a real app.
watchFor: Why naming is not enough: describe how it is used

rows: A mark joining two points. Can be straight, curved, thick or thin. Used to divide, direct the eye or create a border.
A 2D area with a boundary. Geometric (circles, squares) or organic (natural forms).
The area around and between items. White (negative) space gives a design room to breathe.
How a surface looks like it would feel: rough, smooth, grainy.
Hue, value and saturation used to set mood, draw attention and link items.

items.label: Line
items.description: A mark joining two points — straight, curved, thick or thin. Used to divide, direct the eye, or create a border.

items.label: Shape
items.description: A 2D area with a boundary — geometric (circles, squares) or organic (natural forms).

items.label: Space
items.description: The area around and between items. White (negative) space, like the gap around these two faces, gives a design room to breathe.

items.label: Texture
items.description: How a surface looks like it would feel — rough, smooth or grainy.

items.label: Colour
items.description: Hue, value and saturation used to set mood, draw attention and link items.

blocks.text: Worked example: Elements in a streaming app home screen

blocks.html:
Look at any streaming app home screen (Netflix, Stan, Disney+). This is how the five elements are used.

Line — Thin lines separate each row of shows, so rows are easy to scan.

Shape — Rectangular thumbnails repeat across each row; round profile icons stand out from them.

Space and colour — Dark background space makes bright thumbnails stand out; red is used only for the logo and play button.

Texture — Mostly smooth and flat; some thumbnails use photographic texture to add interest.

question.text: Quick check: Which term matches this description? A mark joining two points. Can be straight, curved, thick or thin. Used to divide, direct the eye or create a border.
question.explanation: The term is Line. A mark joining two points. Can be straight, curved, thick or thin. Used to divide, direct the eye or create a border.

blocks.heading: Visual worked example: the streaming home screen

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · LEO THORNE
blocks.text: Clients almost never complain in the language of design elements — they say 'busy' or 'boring' or 'cheap-looking'. Your job is to translate that into 'too much colour contrast' or 'not enough negative space'. Learn the vocabulary and you can diagnose a screen in thirty seconds instead of guessing.

blocks.heading: 🎨 BRIEF
blocks.text: A concert poster needs its date to stand out. The Year 12 syllabus names four principles: balance, emphasis, dominance and unity. Contrast and proportion can create emphasis; proximity and repetition can create unity.
The principles of design: balance, emphasis, dominance, unity

items: Define balance, emphasis, dominance and unity.
Identify contrast and proportion as part of emphasis, and proximity and repetition as part of unity.
Identify principles in a digital product.

blocks.title: Spotting the four principles
blocks.brief: A short clip analysing a concert poster for balance, emphasis, dominance and unity. Suggested source: a teacher-filmed annotated walk-through of a real poster.

rows: How visual weight is spread across a design. Symmetrical (mirror image) or asymmetrical (different items with equal weight).
Making one item stand out as the focal point. Created with contrast (difference in colour, size, shape) and proportion (relative size).
Bright button on a grey page
One item is clearly the most important and is seen first, creating a visual hierarchy.
All parts look like they belong together. Created with proximity (grouping related items) and repetition (reusing colours, fonts, shapes).

items.label: Balance
items.description: How visual weight is spread across a design — symmetrical or asymmetrical. The Taj Mahal's perfectly mirrored facade is a classic example of symmetrical balance.

items.label: Emphasis
items.description: Making one item stand out as the focal point, through contrast and proportion. This basket is lit against a plain background, so it's the only thing the eye can land on.

items.label: Dominance
items.description: One item is clearly the most important and is seen first. Hokusai's wave towers over the boats and even Mount Fuji — there's no doubt what you look at first.

items.label: Unity
items.description: All parts look like they belong together, through proximity and repetition. The Parthenon's columns repeat at equal spacing, so the whole row reads as one structure.

blocks.text: Worked example: Principles on a concert poster

blocks.html:
A poster for a band playing at the Bunbury Entertainment Centre.

Dominance — The band photo takes up half the poster, so it is seen first.

Emphasis — The date is in bright yellow on a black background: strong contrast makes it the second focal point.

Unity — Ticket price, venue and website are grouped together at the bottom (proximity) and use the same font (repetition).

Balance — Asymmetrical: the large photo on the left is balanced by a column of text on the right.

question.text: Quick check: Which term matches this description? How visual weight is spread across a design. Symmetrical (mirror image) or asymmetrical (different items with equal weight).
question.explanation: The term is Balance. How visual weight is spread across a design. Symmetrical (mirror image) or asymmetrical (different items with equal weight).

blocks.heading: Visual worked example: concert poster hierarchy

blocks.html:
Emphasis includes — Contrast: difference in colour, size, shape or tone

Proportion: size of one item compared to another

Unity includes — Proximity: grouping related items close together

Repetition: repeating colours, fonts, shapes or layout

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · LEO THORNE
blocks.text: Elements and principles get mixed up constantly in assessment answers. Quick test I give juniors: if you can point at one thing on the page and name it, it's an element (a colour, a shape). If you're describing a relationship between things — size against size, light against dark — it's a principle. Say that test to yourself before you write the answer.

blocks.heading: 🎨 BRIEF
blocks.text: A bus timetable app came in with white-on-pale-grey text and a client wondering why residents were complaining. Typography choices aren't decoration — on something people read standing at a bus stop in the rain, the wrong font or alignment makes the product unusable, not just unattractive.
Typography: typeface, size, alignment, format, spacing

items: Define the five parts of typography.
Describe typography choices in a digital product.
Justify typography choices for a given audience.

blocks.title: Typography that works
blocks.brief: A short clip comparing a clear and a hard-to-read bus departure screen on typeface, size, alignment, format and spacing. Suggested source: a teacher-filmed side-by-side comparison.
watchFor: What makes text readable at a distance

rows: The design of the letters. Serif (small feet, e.g. Times New Roman) or sans serif (no feet, e.g. Arial).
How big the text is, measured in points (pt). Larger sizes create hierarchy.
How text lines up: left, right, centred or justified.
Styles applied to text: bold, italic, underline, capitals, colour.
Space between letters (kerning, tracking) and lines (leading).

blocks.text: Worked example: Typography on a bus timetable screen

blocks.html:
A digital screen at Bunbury bus station shows the next departures to people standing several metres away.

Typeface — A sans serif typeface, because it is clearer on screens and at a distance.

Size — Route numbers are the largest text so they are found first.

Alignment — Times are right-aligned in a column so the numbers line up.

Format and spacing — Bold for "Departing now"; generous line spacing so rows do not merge.

question.text: Quick check: Which term matches this description? The design of the letters. Serif (small feet, e.g. Times New Roman) or sans serif (no feet, e.g. Arial).
question.explanation: The term is Typeface. The design of the letters. Serif (small feet, e.g. Times New Roman) or sans serif (no feet, e.g. Arial).

blocks.heading: Visual worked example: readable bus departures

blocks.html:
Avoid

  • Using more than two typefaces
  • Long passages in capitals
  • Script fonts for small text
  • Tight line spacing
  • Centred or justified body text

Do

  • Use one typeface for headings and one for body text
  • Build a clear size hierarchy
  • Left-align body text
  • Use bold for emphasis, not underline
  • Keep strong text/background contrast

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · LEO THORNE
blocks.text: Justified text looks 'tidy' to a client's eye and I still have to talk them out of it on anything short — it creates ugly, uneven gaps in narrow columns, which is exactly the opposite of what they wanted. If a client pushes back, show them the gaps in their own copy.

blocks.heading: 🎨 BRIEF
blocks.text: A photo for a website banner came in dead centre, flat, nothing drawing the eye anywhere. The fix wasn't a different photo — it was the rule of thirds, a grid, and real alignment. Compositional rules are what turn a snapshot into a banner someone actually looks at.
Compositional rules: rule of thirds, grid and alignment

items: Describe the rule of thirds.
Describe how a grid and alignment organise content.
Apply compositional rules to improve a layout.

blocks.title: Composition: thirds, grids and alignment
blocks.brief: A short clip fixing a centred banner photo using the rule of thirds, a grid and alignment. Suggested source: a teacher-filmed screen recording in Canva or Photopea.
watchFor: How a grid sets columns and margins

items.definition: Divide the frame into a 3 x 3 grid. Place key items on the lines or where they cross, not in the dead centre.
A set of invisible columns and rows used to place content consistently.
Lining up the edges or centres of items so they look connected and organised.
The first place the eye goes; often placed on a thirds intersection.

blocks.text: Worked example: Fixing a photo for a website banner

blocks.html:
A surfer is placed in the exact centre of a wide website banner, with the text squeezed into the corner.

Problem — A centred subject looks static and leaves awkward space on both sides.

Rule of thirds — Move the surfer to the left third line, facing into the frame.

Grid — Use a 12-column grid: photo across 8 columns, text across the other 4.

Alignment — Left-align the heading, sentence and button on the same column edge.

question.text: Quick check: Which term matches this description? Divide the frame into a 3 x 3 grid. Place key items on the lines or where they cross, not in the dead centre.
question.explanation: The term is Rule of thirds. Divide the frame into a 3 x 3 grid. Place key items on the lines or where they cross, not in the dead centre.

blocks.heading: Visual worked example: repair the banner composition

blocks.text: Laying out a page in four steps

blocks.html:
1

Set a grid — Choose columns and margins before you place anything.

2

Place the focal point — Put the main image or heading on a thirds line.

3

Align everything — Snap text and images to the grid lines.

4

Check the space — Keep equal gaps between items of the same type.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · LEO THORNE
blocks.text: Rule of thirds isn't 'put things slightly off-centre' — it's specific: divide the frame into a 3×3 grid and place the subject or focal point on one of those intersection lines. Vague answers lose marks here because the rule itself is precise.

blocks.text: I had to walk a junior through a pizza delivery app screen this week because they kept writing 'the design is good' — zero marks, every time. Identify, describe, explain, evaluate are four different command words with four different standards, and mixing them up is the single most common way students lose marks on this course.

blocks.text: Worked example: Analysing a pizza delivery app screen

blocks.html:
The order screen: a large pizza photo at the top, a red "Order now" button, and menu items in a grid of same-sized cards.

Dominance — The large photo is seen first; it takes up 40% of the screen.

Emphasis — The red button contrasts with the white background, so it is the call to action.

Unity — Same-sized cards with the same font repeat across the grid.

Weakness and fix — Prices are small and pale grey. Make them bold and darker so they are easy to compare.

blocks.text: A detailed annotation always has three parts: what you changed, which element or principle it uses, and why it serves the design brief. Drop any one of the three and the annotation reads like a caption, not a justification — and captions don't earn marks.

items.why: Names the terms and the effect of unity.

items.text: Big title
One sans serif typeface; heading 36 pt, body 14 pt, left-aligned for easy reading.

blocks.text: Call-out today: a client's laptop 'just feels slow' opening video files. Before I send a tech out, I want you to be able to explain what's actually happening inside the box — CPU, primary memory, secondary storage, volatile vs non-volatile — because half of 'it's slow' complaints are really 'you need more RAM', not a dying CPU.

Explain how CPU and RAM specifications affect performance.

blocks.title: What is inside a laptop?
blocks.brief: A short clip opening up a laptop to show the CPU, RAM and SSD, with a note on what each one does. Suggested source: a teacher-filmed teardown of a spare laptop or a short hardware explainer.
watchFor: Where the RAM and SSD sit
Why a laptop with little RAM feels slow

items.definition: Processes instructions and performs calculations. Speed is measured in GHz; more cores means more tasks at once.
Memory the CPU uses directly. RAM is temporary (volatile): it is cleared when power is off. ROM stores start-up instructions permanently.
Stores files and programs permanently (non-volatile), e.g. SSD, HDD, USB flash drive, memory card.
Loses its data when power is turned off.

blocks.title: Inside the Computer
blocks.caption: Before the worked example, watch a file move from storage into RAM and through the CPU.

pauseQuestions.question: Name the two input devices shown, and one more input device that is not shown.
pauseQuestions.answer: Keyboard and mouse. Others include a microphone, webcam, touchscreen, scanner or game controller.

pauseQuestions.question: Why do the SSD's packets reach the RAM before the HDD's?
pauseQuestions.answer: An SSD stores data on flash memory chips with no moving parts. An HDD has to spin a disk and move a read arm to find the data, so it is much slower.

pauseQuestions.question: What happens to the data in RAM when the computer is switched off?
pauseQuestions.answer: It is lost. RAM is volatile, so it only holds data while it has power. That is why work has to be saved to storage.

pauseQuestions.question: Why do packets keep moving back and forth between the CPU and the RAM?
pauseQuestions.answer: The CPU fetches instructions and data from RAM, processes them, then writes the results back to RAM.

pauseQuestions.question: Which component turns the result into a picture? Name the two output devices shown.
pauseQuestions.answer: The graphics card (GPU) makes the picture. The output devices are the monitor and the speakers.

blocks.title: Put the video playback in order
blocks.instruction: Tap what happens when you double-click a saved video.
items: The file is stored on the SSD.
The file and the video player are loaded into RAM.
The CPU processes the instructions to decode and play the video.
Power off: RAM is cleared, but the file is still on the SSD.
blocks.explanation: Storage holds the file, RAM holds what is in use, the CPU processes it. RAM is volatile; the SSD is not.

blocks.title: Primary or secondary?
blocks.instruction: Which type of memory does each statement describe?

items.text: Loses its contents when the power goes off.
Keeps your files with the power off.
items.why: Non-volatile storage keeps data without power.

items.text: Holds the data being used right now, so the CPU can reach it fast.
items.why: Primary memory is the CPU's working space.

items.text: Typically 256 GB to several TB.
items.why: Secondary storage is much larger than RAM.

items.text: Very fast but high cost per GB.
items.why: RAM is much faster and costs more per GB.

items.text: Where a saved video file lives long term.
items.why: Files are stored long term on secondary storage.

blocks.title: Two laptops
blocks.intro: Laptop A: 4-core 2.4 GHz CPU, 16 GB RAM, 256 GB SSD. Laptop B: 2-core 1.6 GHz CPU, 8 GB RAM, 1 TB HDD. A student needs one for school.

steps.situation: She edits short videos for a media project.
steps.prompt: Which statement best explains which laptop suits her?

choices.text: Laptop A: video editing loads large clips into RAM, and 16 GB with a faster 4-core CPU copes better than 8 GB.
choices.feedback: It links RAM and CPU specs to the task.

choices.text: Laptop B, because it stores more videos.
choices.feedback: That is secondary storage, not what makes editing smooth.

choices.text: Laptop A, because it is newer.
choices.feedback: Age is not a specification. Name the specs and the effect.

steps.situation: She compares the storage of the two laptops.

choices.text: B holds four times more (1 TB against 256 GB), but A's SSD is faster and more durable than B's HDD.
choices.feedback: It compares capacity and speed or durability, as the marker wants.

choices.text: B has more storage.
choices.feedback: Only one feature, and no comparison of speed.

choices.text: They both store files.
choices.feedback: A comparison needs differences, not a shared feature.

blocks.title: Check your understanding
blocks.instruction: Answer first, then flip.

cards.front: What does the CPU do?
cards.back: It processes instructions and performs calculations. Speed is measured in GHz and more cores means more tasks at once.

cards.front: What does volatile mean?
cards.back: Loses its data when the power is turned off, like RAM.

cards.front: Why might 8 GB of RAM be slow for video editing?
cards.back: Large clips fill the RAM quickly, so the computer falls back on slower storage and lags.

blocks.heading: Sparky's warning
blocks.text: Volatile is the word that trips people up every year. It just means 'loses its contents when the power goes', which is RAM. If a student cannot tell me which one is volatile, they cannot yet explain why unsaved work disappears in a blackout.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Explain why a laptop with 8 GB of RAM may be slow for video editing. (2 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark: "It cannot store many videos."
cards.text: That is secondary storage, not RAM.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "Video editing loads large clips into RAM; with only 8 GB it fills quickly, so the computer uses slower storage instead and lags." RAM, the task and the effect.

blocks.title: Match the OS to its use
blocks.instruction: Which operating system does each description fit best?

items.text: A school laptop running the widest range of business and school software.
items.why: Windows runs the widest range of software.

items.text: A graphic design studio's iMac that works closely with other Apple devices.
items.why: macOS runs on Apple computers and is common in creative industries.

items.text: An iPhone, with apps only from the App Store.
items.why: iOS is only on Apple mobile devices.

items.text: A Samsung phone and a smart TV made by different brands.
items.why: Android is used by many manufacturers.

items.text: A free, stable web server that is highly customisable.
items.why: Linux is open source and common on servers.

rows: Runs the widest range of software
Works closely with other Apple devices
Apps only from the App Store

blocks.title: Open source or proprietary?
blocks.instruction: Sort each feature.

items.text: Source code can be viewed and changed.
items.why: That is the definition of open source.

items.text: Owned by a company, with closed source code.
Linux, and the core of Android.
Windows, macOS and iOS.
items.why: All three are owned by a company.

blocks.title: Windows or Linux?
blocks.intro: A small business is choosing between Windows laptops and Linux laptops for its five staff.

steps.situation: The owner asks for one real advantage of Linux for the business.

choices.text: It is free, so the business saves licence fees on five laptops.
choices.feedback: A real advantage linked to the business.

choices.text: Linux is cool.
choices.feedback: Not an advantage, and not linked to the business.

choices.text: Linux has no advantages.
choices.feedback: It does: it is free and customisable.

steps.situation: The owner asks for one real disadvantage.

choices.text: Support is mostly from the community, so there is no guaranteed help when something breaks during the working day.
choices.feedback: A disadvantage that applies to a business needing reliable support.

choices.text: It costs a lot.
choices.feedback: Linux is generally free, so this is wrong.

choices.text: It cannot run any software.
choices.feedback: It runs a lot of software, though some business programs are Windows-only.

blocks.title: Check your understanding
blocks.instruction: Answer first, then flip.

cards.front: Name two purposes of an OS.
cards.back: Any two of: manage memory and the CPU, manage files and storage, control peripherals via drivers, provide a user interface, run applications, provide security.

cards.front: Why is 'Windows and Android' a wrong answer to 'purposes of an OS'?
cards.back: Those are types of OS, not purposes.

blocks.heading: Sparky's warning
blocks.text: Do not just say Linux is free and proprietary is not. Free also usually means community-supported, which is an advantage for a hobbyist and a real disadvantage for a business that needs guaranteed support.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Describe two purposes of an operating system. (4 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark: "Windows and Android."
cards.text: These are types, not purposes.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "It manages files, so users can save, open and organise them in folders. It controls peripherals through drivers, so a printer works when plugged in." Two purposes, each with how it helps.

cards.heading: Scenario: The five-laptop business
cards.text: A small business is choosing between Windows laptops and Linux laptops for its five staff. Answer the questions below using this scenario.

question.text: Describe two purposes of an operating system.
Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of Linux for the business.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Advantage explained (e.g. free, so no licence cost for five laptops)
2 marks – Disadvantage explained (e.g. some business software only runs on Windows, and staff may need training)

cards.heading: Purposes, not types
cards.text: Describe what an OS does, such as managing files or controlling peripherals through drivers.

cards.heading: Pair the advantage and disadvantage to the client
cards.text: Free but community-supported is the classic Linux pair.

cards.text: At least 6/8 on the practice questions. If not, reread the key terms and test tip.

items.definition: Whether software runs correctly on a given hardware and operating system.
May not install or may crash, because the new OS no longer supports it; no longer receives security updates.
May not install or may run slowly, because the hardware is below the minimum requirements.
The lowest specifications (CPU, RAM, storage, OS, graphics) the software needs to run.
Cost (budget), specifications (performance) and user needs (what the user will do with it).

blocks.title: Game versus laptop
blocks.instruction: The game needs 16 GB RAM, 60 GB free storage, a dedicated graphics card and Windows 10 64-bit or later. Her laptop has 8 GB RAM, 200 GB free, integrated graphics and Windows 11 64-bit. Does each specification meet the requirement?

items.text: RAM: 8 GB against 16 GB required.
items.why: 8 GB is below the 16 GB minimum.

items.text: Storage: 200 GB free against 60 GB required.
Graphics: integrated against a dedicated card required.
items.why: Integrated graphics does not meet a dedicated card requirement.

items.text: Operating system: Windows 11 64-bit against Windows 10 64-bit or later.

blocks.title: The purchase decision
blocks.instruction: Tap the four steps for choosing new computers in order.
items: User needs: what will they do, where and how often?
Software: list it and its minimum requirements.
Specifications: choose above the minimum, with room to grow.
Cost: compare options within the budget.
blocks.explanation: Needs first, then software, then specs, then cost. Cost alone is never a full answer.

blocks.title: The dental practice
blocks.intro: A dental practice still uses booking software made for Windows 7. It is buying new Windows 11 computers for $1200 each.

steps.situation: The practice manager asks what could go wrong.
steps.prompt: Which compatibility issue is specific to this practice?

choices.text: The old Windows 7 booking software may not install or may crash on Windows 11, and it no longer receives security updates.
choices.feedback: It names the issue for this setup, in both directions.

choices.text: Computers are sometimes incompatible.
choices.feedback: A general statement, not specific to the practice.

choices.text: Nothing. New computers run everything.
choices.feedback: Old software may not run on a new OS.

steps.situation: She asks what to consider before choosing the new computers.

choices.text: Check the booking software's minimum requirements against the specifications, and match them to what staff do, not just the cost.
choices.feedback: Specifications, user needs and cost all matter.

choices.text: Buy the cheapest.
choices.feedback: Cost alone is never a full answer.

choices.text: Buy the newest model.
choices.feedback: Newest does not guarantee it runs the practice's software.

blocks.title: Check your understanding
blocks.instruction: Answer first, then flip.

cards.front: What are minimum requirements?
cards.back: The lowest specifications (CPU, RAM, storage, OS, graphics) the software needs to run.

cards.front: What goes wrong when new software meets older hardware?
cards.back: It may not install, or may run slowly, because the hardware is below the minimum requirements.

cards.front: What goes wrong when old software meets a new OS?
cards.back: It may not install or may crash, and it no longer receives security updates.

blocks.heading: Sparky's warning
blocks.text: Everyone checks whether the new software will run on the old machine and forgets the other direction: will the old, specialised software still run on new hardware and a new OS. Always check both ways.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Identify which specifications do not meet the requirements. (2 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark: "It is too slow."
cards.text: Does not name a specification.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "RAM (8 GB is below the required 16 GB) and graphics (integrated, but a dedicated card is required)." The specification and the gap.

question.text: Explain two considerations when choosing the new computers.

cards.text: Old software on new hardware, and new software on old hardware.

blocks.heading: 🔧 JOB TICKET
blocks.text: 3am call-out: a server shut itself down twice this week and the client lost power mid-task with no warning. This is exactly the job a UPS and proper environmental control exist to prevent — today's about recognising the fix before the client has to call me at 3am again.

Describe steps to solve no sound, frozen devices and projector problems.

blocks.title: Fixing it before the call-out
blocks.brief: A short clip fixing the three common faults (no sound, a frozen screen, a projector with no picture) and showing a UPS in a server cabinet. Suggested source: a teacher-filmed demonstration using a school classroom setup.
watchFor: The order the checks are made in
What a UPS does in a blackout
Why the server room needs cooling

items.definition: A battery unit that keeps equipment running during a power failure long enough to save work and shut down safely. Also protects against power surges.
Keeping equipment cool with air-conditioning and ventilation, because heat damages components and causes shutdowns.
Finding and fixing a problem by checking the simplest causes first.

cards.heading: UPS
cards.text: Server stays on during a short blackout. Time to save work and shut down safely. Stops data loss and file damage. Protects against surges.

cards.heading: Temperature control
cards.text: Servers produce a lot of heat. Overheating slows or shuts down the CPU and shortens component life. Keep vents clear of dust.

blocks.title: A logical troubleshooting order
blocks.instruction: Tap the four steps in order.
items: Describe the problem and when it happens.
Check the simplest causes first, such as cables, volume and power.
Try one fix at a time and test after each.
Restart, then escalate if it is still not fixed.
blocks.explanation: Simplest first, one change at a time, and test as you go.

blocks.title: Which fault does this fix?
blocks.instruction: Tap the problem each step helps solve.

items.text: Click the speaker icon and check the output is the laptop speakers, not a disconnected Bluetooth headset.
items.why: Checking the output device is a no-sound fix.

items.text: Open Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc) and end the frozen app.
items.why: Ending the frozen application is a frozen-device fix.

items.text: Press Windows+P and choose Duplicate.
items.why: It sends the laptop's display to the projector.

items.text: Check the cable is secure at both ends and the projector's input is selected.
items.why: Cable and input selection are the first projector checks.

items.text: Check wireless mouse batteries, then restart.
items.why: A dead wireless mouse can look like a frozen device.

items.text: Check mute and volume, then restart the app.
items.why: Mute and volume are the first no-sound checks.

blocks.title: Maintenance checklist
blocks.instruction: Turn on the good habits and turn off the risky ones.
blocks.explanation: Regular updates, scans and backups keep a computer healthy and your files safe.

blocks.title: The accounting firm's server
blocks.intro: A small accounting firm keeps its server in a storeroom with no windows. Last summer the server shut down twice on hot days, and a blackout corrupted a file.

steps.situation: The partner asks how a UPS would have helped in the blackout.

choices.text: The UPS battery keeps the server running for a few minutes, giving time to save files and shut down safely, so the file would not have been corrupted.
choices.feedback: It explains the function, not just 'it would have helped'.

choices.text: A UPS stops the server ever losing power.
choices.feedback: It manages the loss, it does not eliminate it. The battery only lasts minutes.

choices.text: It would have helped.
choices.feedback: No explanation of what the UPS actually does.

steps.situation: The server keeps shutting down on hot days.

choices.text: Add air-conditioning or ventilation to the storeroom, and keep the server's vents clear of dust.
choices.feedback: Both strategies address heat, which is the cause.

choices.text: Buy a bigger monitor.
choices.feedback: Unrelated to overheating.

choices.text: Move the server somewhere with no power outlets.
choices.feedback: It would not run, and does not address heat.

blocks.title: Check your understanding
blocks.instruction: Answer first, then flip.

cards.front: What is a UPS?
cards.back: A battery unit that keeps equipment running during a power failure long enough to save work and shut down safely. It also protects against surges.

cards.front: Why does a server shut down on a hot day?
cards.back: Heat damages components and causes shutdowns. Cooling and ventilation prevent it.

blocks.heading: Sparky's warning
blocks.text: A UPS does not keep the power on forever. It buys you minutes to save your work and shut down safely, or bridges a short outage. If an answer says a UPS 'stops the computer losing power', that is not quite it.

blocks.intro: Describe one step to fix a laptop with no sound. (2 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark: "Fix the settings."
cards.text: Which settings?

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "Click the speaker icon and check the output is set to the laptop speakers, not a disconnected Bluetooth headset." A specific step.

cards.text: A small accounting firm keeps its server in a storeroom with no windows. Last summer the server shut down twice on hot days, and a blackout corrupted a file. Answer the questions below using this scenario.

question.text: Describe two strategies to stop the server shutting down on hot days.

cards.heading: Explain the UPS properly
cards.text: Battery gives time to save and shut down safely. It manages the power loss, it does not remove it.

cards.heading: Mention heat and cooling
cards.text: Hot-day shutdowns are a temperature problem.

items.definition: Using digital technologies safely, responsibly and respectfully, and understanding your rights and responsibilities online.

blocks.title: Four terms, four answers
blocks.instruction: Read the front, answer out loud, then flip.

cards.front: What is digital citizenship?
cards.back: Using digital technologies safely, responsibly and respectfully, and understanding your rights and responsibilities online.

cards.front: What is a digital footprint?
cards.back: The permanent record of everything you post, share, like and search online, including what others post about you.

cards.front: Why is posting a friend's photo without asking irresponsible?
cards.back: The friend did not agree to it joining their digital footprint, and the photo can be copied even if you later delete it.

cards.front: Who must take 'reasonable steps' to stop under-16s having accounts (from 10 December 2025)?
cards.back: The age-restricted social media platforms. The obligation and penalties apply to the platforms, not to the young person or their parents.

blocks.title: Sort Jordan's choices
blocks.instruction: Jordan (17) is posting about a party. Is each choice responsible or risky?

items.text: Posts a group photo without asking anyone first.
items.why: Others did not give permission, and the photo stays in their digital footprint.

items.text: Checks his privacy settings before posting.
items.why: Only approved followers see the post, which limits the audience.

items.text: Tags the party's location while it is happening.
items.why: Strangers can see where a group of young people is right now.

items.text: Deletes a friend's rude comment and messages them privately.
items.why: It stops the harm spreading and deals with it privately.

items.text: Reshares a shocking story without checking if it is true.
items.why: Unchecked information can spread false claims and hurt real people.

items.text: Credits the photographer when he shares a photo they took.
items.why: Crediting others is part of respectful, responsible sharing.

question.text: Jordan wants to post a group photo but has not asked the other people. What is the most responsible first step?
options: Ask the people in the photo before posting it.
Post it now and remove it if someone complains.
Tag everyone so they find out after it is posted.
question.explanation: Ask permission first. Other people should have a say in what is added to their digital footprint.

cards.heading: Do
cards.text: Pause and think about the audience. Ask before sharing someone's photo. Check privacy settings. Verify information before sharing. Report harmful content.

cards.heading: Avoid
cards.text: Posting your school, phone number or live location publicly. Accepting requests from people you do not know. Posting while angry. Sharing someone's work without credit or using their account.

blocks.title: Elara's case file: the public TikTok
blocks.intro: Elara's Year 10 student has a public account showing her school uniform and a local park. Make the calls that reduce her risk.

steps.situation: Her profile photo shows her school uniform with the crest clearly visible.
steps.prompt: What is the best first change?

choices.text: Swap to a photo with no uniform or crest, and remove the school from her bio.
choices.feedback: Removing identifying details makes it harder for strangers to work out who she is and where she is during the day.

choices.text: Leave it, because the account is already popular.
choices.feedback: Popularity does not reduce the risk. It means more strangers can see the identifying details.

choices.text: Add a filter over the crest.
choices.feedback: Filters are easy to avoid and the uniform can still be recognised.

steps.situation: Her videos are often filmed at the same local park, and she posts them as she films.

choices.text: Turn off location tags and post after she has left the park.
choices.feedback: Delaying posts and removing location tags stops strangers learning where she is right now.

choices.text: Keep tagging the park so friends can join her.
choices.feedback: A live location tells strangers exactly where to find her.

choices.text: Only tag the park in her Stories, not the main feed.
choices.feedback: Stories are still visible to a public audience, so the risk stays.

steps.situation: A stranger comments asking which school she goes to.
steps.prompt: What is the most responsible response?

choices.text: Do not reply, block the account and report it.
choices.feedback: Not engaging, blocking and reporting protects her and helps the platform act.

choices.text: Reply with the school name because he seems friendly.
choices.feedback: Giving personal information to a stranger is exactly the risk digital citizenship warns about.

choices.text: Delete the comment and say nothing.
choices.feedback: Deleting alone does not stop the stranger or warn the platform.

blocks.heading: Elara's reminder
blocks.text: Your digital footprint includes what other people post about you, too. Ask before sharing a photo, and remember that deleting a post cannot guarantee every copy disappears.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Explain one consequence of posting an inappropriate photo online. (2 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark: "You could get in trouble."
cards.text: Too general. It does not say how or why.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "The photo becomes part of your digital footprint and can be copied or screenshotted, so it may be seen by a future employer even after you delete it." A consequence, plus how it happens.

blocks.heading: Your turn
blocks.text: In your notes, define digital citizenship and plan two realistic changes for the student in the opening case. Explain how each change reduces risk.

question.text: Define digital citizenship.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Defines digital citizenship as using technology safely, responsibly and respectfully, including rights and responsibilities
1 mark – States it is "being good online"

question.text: Describe two changes the student could make to use social networking more responsibly.

cards.heading: Define it
cards.text: Digital citizenship is using technology safely, responsibly and respectfully, while understanding online rights and responsibilities.

cards.heading: Be specific
cards.text: Give actions such as asking permission or removing identifying details, then explain how each one reduces risk.

cards.heading: Aim for
cards.text: At least 5/6 on the practice questions. If you miss it, review the key terms and the Do/Avoid cards, then try again.

blocks.heading: 📋 CASE FILE
blocks.text: Two unrelated cases on my desk that both come back to the same syllabus point: naming the exact form of cyberbullying — harassment, exclusion, impersonation, outing — and separately, a work group chat that's eaten someone's evenings. Precision matters in both; 'bullying' isn't specific enough for a case file.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

cards.heading: Describe strategies to manage or limit cyberbullying.
Explain positive and negative impacts of digital technologies on work-life balance.

blocks.title: Cyberbullying: what to do next
blocks.brief: A short clip showing a student taking the four response steps: do not reply, keep evidence, block and report, get help. Suggested source: an eSafety Commissioner video on dealing with cyberbullying.

items.definition: Using digital technology to deliberately and repeatedly hurt, threaten or embarrass someone.
Repeatedly sending offensive or threatening messages.
Deliberately leaving someone out of an online group or chat.
Pretending to be someone else online to damage their reputation.
Sharing someone's private information or images without permission.
Dividing time and energy between work and personal life in a healthy way.

cards.heading: Harassment
cards.text: Repeated offensive or threatening messages.

cards.heading: Exclusion
cards.text: Deliberately leaving someone out of a group or chat.

cards.heading: Impersonation
cards.text: Pretending to be someone else to damage their reputation.

cards.heading: Outing
cards.text: Sharing private information or images without permission.

blocks.title: Which form is it?
blocks.instruction: Read each situation and tap the form of cyberbullying.

items.text: A student gets 30 abusive messages in a night from different accounts.
items.why: Repeated unwanted, offensive contact is harassment.

items.text: Everyone in the class is added to a new group chat except one person, on purpose.
items.why: Deliberately leaving someone out is exclusion.

items.text: Someone makes a fake account with a classmate's photo and posts insults as them.
items.why: Pretending to be the victim to damage their reputation is impersonation.

items.text: A private screenshot of someone's personal message is shared with the whole year group.
items.why: Sharing private information without consent is outing.

items.text: A gamer is sent threats every time he streams.

blocks.title: The four-step response
blocks.alt: Four steps in order: do not reply, keep evidence, block and report, get help.

blocks.title: Put the response in order
blocks.instruction: Tap the four steps in the order a student should take them.
items: Do not respond to the bully.
Collect evidence with screenshots showing date and username.
Block the accounts and report them to the platform.
Tell a trusted adult, and report to eSafety if the platform does not act within 48 hours.
blocks.explanation: Evidence comes before blocking, because blocking or deletion can remove what you need to prove it.

question.text: Someone sets up a fake profile using a classmate's photo and posts insults as her. Which form is this?
question.explanation: Pretending to be someone else online to damage their reputation is impersonation.

blocks.title: Positive or negative?
blocks.instruction: Sort each impact of digital technology on work-life balance.

items.text: Working from home saves two hours of travel a day.
items.why: Saved travel time can go to family, rest or study.

items.text: Work emails arrive at 10 pm and staff feel they must reply.
items.why: It makes people always contactable and cuts into rest and family time.

items.text: Flexible hours let a parent work around school pick-up.
items.why: Technology allows work to fit around family commitments.

items.text: Scrolling on a phone in bed replaces sleep.
items.why: Screen time displaces sleep and exercise.

items.text: Video calls keep a worker in touch with family while away.
items.why: Staying connected is a positive impact on personal life.

items.text: Mostly online contact leaves a worker feeling isolated.
items.why: Less face-to-face contact can lead to isolation.

blocks.heading: Elara's rule
blocks.text: Each form of cyberbullying has a distinct mechanism: harassment is repeated unwanted contact, exclusion is deliberately leaving someone out, impersonation is pretending to be them, outing is exposing private information. Name the mechanism, or the strategy you recommend will not fit the problem.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Explain one negative impact of mobile devices on work-life balance. (2 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark: "Phones are addictive."
cards.text: Not linked to work-life balance.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "Work emails arrive on the phone at night, so staff feel they must reply, which cuts into family time and rest." A named impact tied to work-life balance.

cards.heading: Scenario: The supermarket group chat
cards.text: A Year 11 student works part-time at a supermarket. The manager messages shifts in a group chat, often late at night. Two co-workers have started posting jokes about her in the chat. Answer the questions below using this scenario.

question.text: Identify the form of cyberbullying and describe one strategy she could use to manage it.
question.explanation:
3 marks – Identifies a form (harassment or denigration) (1) and describes a strategy with how it helps (2)
2 marks – Identifies a form and states a strategy
1 mark – Identifies a form only

question.text: Explain one negative impact of the group chat on her work-life balance.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Explains that late messages mean she is always "on call" and work intrudes on rest or study time
1 mark – States a negative impact with no link to work-life balance

cards.heading: Name the form first
cards.text: Harassment, exclusion, impersonation or outing, then choose a strategy that fits.

cards.heading: Link to work-life balance
cards.text: Name the actual impact, such as lost sleep or missed family time, not just 'it is bad'.

cards.heading: Aim for
cards.text: At least 4/5 on the practice questions. If not, reread the key terms and test tip.

blocks.heading: 📋 CASE FILE
blocks.text: A storm hit Bunbury and the local paper broke the story on social media before their own website updated. That's not a one-off — it's the whole shift from traditional publication to user-created, instantly distributed content, and it's exactly what reshaped how this industry works.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

cards.heading: Compare traditional and social publication of information.
Explain the role of mobile devices in this change.

blocks.title: How news changed: print to phone
blocks.brief: A short explainer comparing how a news story travels through a newsroom with how a social post spreads. Suggested source: an ABC Education or similar media-literacy clip, or a teacher-filmed example using a local story.
watchFor: Who checks the story before it is published
How fast it reaches an audience
Where the audience sees it first

items.definition: Online platforms where users create profiles, connect with others and share content.
Information produced and checked by publishers (newspapers, TV, radio, books) and distributed on a schedule.
How information reaches the audience: print, broadcast, or shared online.
Posts, videos and comments made by ordinary users rather than professional publishers.

blocks.title: A storm hits Bunbury: 1995 vs today
blocks.alt: Two lanes. In 1995 a story moves slowly from journalist to editor to print to doorstep. Today a resident's post reaches everyone in minutes.

cards.heading: Gain
cards.text: Information spreads instantly and anyone can report what they see.

cards.heading: Loss
cards.text: Posts are not checked before sharing, so false information and old videos spread too.

blocks.title: Match the feature to social networking
blocks.instruction: Tap a feature on the left, then tap how social networking handles it.

right: Instant
Anyone with a phone
Often not checked
Free, paid for by advertising
Comments, shares and creates

blocks.explanation: Social networking changed news from something you receive to something anyone can publish, instantly and unchecked.

blocks.title: Check your comparison
blocks.instruction: Try the answer before you flip.

cards.front: Which is faster to publish: newspaper or social network? Why?
cards.back: Social networking. Anyone can post instantly from a phone, while a newspaper is edited and printed on a schedule.

cards.front: Why is a newspaper story usually more reliable?
cards.back: Editors check it before it is published. Social posts are often shared with no checking.

cards.front: How do mobile devices change how people receive news?
cards.back: Push notifications and feeds deliver news instantly wherever people are, without buying a paper or waiting for the 6 pm bulletin.

cards.front: What is the real shift in distribution?
cards.back: Distribution used to be controlled by publishers. Now anyone with a phone is a distributor.

blocks.title: Traditional or social?
blocks.instruction: Which type of publication does each statement describe?

items.text: An editor checks facts before the story goes out.
items.why: Editing and checking before publishing is a feature of traditional publication.

items.text: A resident posts a video of the storm within minutes.
items.why: User-created content posted instantly is social networking.

items.text: Readers pay for a subscription or a printed paper.
The audience comments, shares and creates content.
items.why: On social networks the audience takes part, not just receives.

items.text: News arrives on a schedule, such as the morning paper.
Free to use and paid for by advertising.
items.why: Social platforms are free for the audience and funded by ads.

blocks.heading: Elara's point
blocks.text: The real shift is not that social media is faster. Distribution used to be controlled by the publisher, and now anyone with a phone is a distributor. That one change explains speed, reach and the loss of editorial gatekeeping.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Compare how news is published on social networks and in newspapers. (4 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark: "Social media is faster."
cards.text: Only one side and one feature.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "Newspapers are checked by editors before printing, so they are more reliable but slower; social networks let anyone post instantly from a phone, so news is faster but may be false." Both sides, with a linking word.

cards.heading: Scenario: The newspaper that went online
cards.text: A regional newspaper has closed its printed edition and now publishes only on its website and Facebook page. Answer the questions below using this scenario.

question.text: Explain one reason the newspaper made this change.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Explains a reason (e.g. fewer people buy printed papers because they read free news on social media, so print costs are no longer covered)
1 mark – States a reason with no explanation

question.text: Explain one impact of mobile devices on how people receive local news.
question.explanation:
3 marks – Explains an impact in detail linked to mobile devices (e.g. push notifications and feeds deliver news instantly wherever people are)
2 marks – Describes an impact
1 mark – States an impact

cards.heading: Compare means both sides
cards.text: Name a feature for traditional and for social networking, and join them with a linking word like 'whereas'.

cards.heading: Mobile devices
cards.text: Name the actual change, such as push notifications delivering news anywhere.

cards.heading: Aim for
cards.text: At least 4/5 on the practice questions. If not, reread the key terms and test tip.

blocks.heading: 📋 CASE FILE
blocks.text: A student's in hot water for using copyrighted material and swears they thought 'private use' covered it. Half my case files are exactly this misunderstanding — the Copyright Act 1968, fair dealing, private use and moral rights don't mean what people assume they mean.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

cards.heading: State the purpose of the Copyright Act 1968.
Describe fair dealing, private use and moral rights.
Apply the Act to a scenario.

blocks.title: Copyright in 3 minutes
blocks.brief: A short Australian explainer on what copyright protects, what fair dealing allows and what moral rights mean. Suggested source: Australian Copyright Council or Smartcopying material for schools.
watchFor: What counts as a protected work

items.definition: Australian law that protects creators' original works (text, images, music, film, software). Protection is automatic: no registration is needed.
Using a reasonable portion of a work without permission for specific purposes: research or study, criticism or review, parody or satire, reporting news, or professional advice.
Limited copying for your own use, e.g. copying music you own to your phone, or recording a TV show to watch later.
The creator's right to be named (attribution), not to have others named as the creator (false attribution), and not to have the work treated in a harmful way (integrity).

blocks.title: Can I use this work?
blocks.alt: A four-step check: is it a created work, do you have permission, is an exception met, and always credit the creator.

blocks.title: Fair dealing: the five purposes
blocks.intro: Using a reasonable portion without permission is only allowed for these.

cards.heading: Research or study
cards.text: A short clip in a marked class assignment.

cards.heading: Criticism or review
cards.text: Quoting a scene to review a film.

cards.heading: Parody or satire
cards.text: A sketch that mocks a song.

cards.heading: Reporting news
cards.text: Showing a clip in a news report.

cards.heading: Professional advice
cards.text: A lawyer copying a case to advise a client.

blocks.title: Four uses of a song
blocks.instruction: A song by an Australian artist is used in four ways. Tap the outcome for each.

items.text: Using 20 seconds in a class video marked by your teacher.
items.why: Research or study, a reasonable portion, kept for assessment.

items.text: Copying a song you bought onto your own phone.
items.why: Limited copying for your own use is private use.

items.text: Uploading that class video to a public YouTube channel.
items.why: It is no longer for study, so it needs permission or a licence.

items.text: Remixing the song and posting it with your name as the creator.
items.why: It infringes copyright and the artist's moral right of attribution.

blocks.title: Myth or fact?
blocks.instruction: Decide if the claim is true, then flip to check.

cards.front: "It is on the internet, so it is free."
cards.back: Online works are still protected by copyright.

cards.front: "If I credit the creator, I can use it."
cards.back: Credit is required but it is not permission.

cards.front: "Under 10 seconds is always fine."
cards.back: There is no safe number of seconds. It depends on purpose and portion.

cards.front: "I changed it a bit, so it is mine."
cards.back: A changed work can still infringe copyright.

question.text: Copyright protection is automatic, so a creator does not need to register their work.
question.explanation: Protection under the Copyright Act 1968 applies automatically when an original work is created.

question.text: Which moral right is the right to be named as the creator?
question.explanation: Attribution is the right to be named as creator. Integrity protects the work from harmful treatment, and false attribution stops someone else being named.

blocks.heading: Elara's warning
blocks.text: Private use is much narrower than people think. It does not mean 'I did not make money' or 'I only showed my friends'. Most student infringements fail because they assumed private use covered far more than it does.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Explain whether fair dealing applies to a clip used in a school assignment. (2 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark: "Yes, because it is only a small part."
cards.text: Size alone does not decide it.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "Yes. The clip is a reasonable portion used for research or study, so fair dealing applies while it is only used for assessment." Names the purpose, the portion and the limit.

cards.heading: Scenario: The fundraiser T-shirt
cards.text: A student designs a T-shirt for a school fundraiser using a cartoon character copied from a website. The shirts are sold to parents. Answer the questions below using this scenario.

question.text: Explain why the student has infringed copyright.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Explains that the character is protected automatically and was reproduced and sold without permission; fair dealing does not cover selling products
1 mark – States that permission was not asked

question.text: Describe the moral rights of the cartoon's creator.
question.explanation:
1 mark per right, up to 3
3 marks – Attribution: right to be named as creator. False attribution: right not to have someone else named. Integrity: right not to have the work treated in a harmful way.

cards.heading: Copyright is automatic
cards.text: No registration needed. Fair dealing is only for the five listed purposes.

cards.heading: Moral rights are separate
cards.text: Attribution, false attribution and integrity. Do not mix them up with ownership.

cards.heading: Aim for
cards.text: At least 4/5 on the practice questions. If not, reread the key terms and myths.

blocks.heading: Up next
blocks.text: Next lesson: referencing techniques and acknowledging the IP owner.

blocks.heading: 📋 CASE FILE
blocks.text: Every case file I close ends the same way — an intellectual property acknowledgement that has to be done properly or the whole report is worthless. APA 7, in-text citations, acknowledgement versus full referencing: get the technique right, because 'I mentioned where it came from' isn't the same as a correct citation.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

cards.heading: Explain why IP owners must be acknowledged.
Write a reference in one consistent technique (APA 7).
Acknowledge images, music and video in a digital product.

blocks.title: APA 7 referencing in 3 minutes
blocks.brief: A short walk-through building one website reference and one image reference in APA 7. Suggested source: a university library APA 7 guide video, or a teacher-filmed screen recording.
watchFor: The order of the five parts
Where the full stops and brackets go
How a photograph reference differs from a website one

items.definition: Creations of the mind, such as writing, images, music, software and designs, that belong to their creator.
Naming the creator and source of work you have used, on or with your product.
A consistent set of rules for listing sources, e.g. APA or Harvard.
A short reference in the body of the work, e.g. (eSafety Commissioner, 2026).

blocks.alt: A reference split into five coloured parts: author, year, title, source, URL.

blocks.title: Creative Commons
blocks.instruction: Tap each to see what you must do.

cards.front: What does CC BY require?
cards.back: You must credit the creator.

cards.front: What does NC mean?
cards.back: No commercial use. You cannot use it to make money.

cards.front: What must you do before using a free image or track?
cards.back: Check its licence. Free to download does not mean free of conditions.

cards.front: What is the difference?
cards.back: Acknowledgement can be a simple credit line. Referencing follows an exact technique like APA 7. If the question names the technique, use that format.

blocks.heading: Elara's rule
blocks.text: Acknowledgement and referencing are not interchangeable terms in a marking key. If the question names the technique, you must use that exact format.

blocks.title: The real estate agency
blocks.intro: A small real estate agency saves property photos, contracts and floor plans for 50 houses on one shared drive with no folders.

steps.situation: Describe a folder structure they could use.

choices.text: A folder for each property, with subfolders for Photos, Contracts and Floor plans, so everything for a house is together.
choices.feedback: A clear hierarchy matched to the agency.

choices.text: One big folder called Stuff.
choices.feedback: That is the problem.

choices.text: Folders named by file type only, mixing all 50 houses.
choices.feedback: Hard to find a single house's files.

steps.situation: Explain a benefit of a naming convention.

choices.text: Staff can find a property's files quickly, and version numbers stop old contracts being mistaken for current ones.
choices.feedback: Two benefits linked to the agency.

choices.text: Files look pretty.
choices.feedback: Not a real benefit.

choices.text: It uses less storage.
choices.feedback: Naming does not change size.

blocks.title: Build a Real Folder Structure
blocks.software: File Explorer or Finder (or your school's cloud drive)
blocks.intro: Build an actual folder structure for the wedding videographer's agency from this lesson — not a diagram of one, a real set of folders you can navigate.
steps: In your course folder, create a top-level folder named Agency-Files.
Inside it, create one subfolder per client using a consistent naming convention, e.g. 2026-06-ClientSurname (date then surname, so folders sort chronologically).
Inside each client folder, create subfolders for the stages of the job: 01-RawFootage, 02-Edits, 03-FinalDelivery.

Create at least 10 dummy files (empty text files are fine) spread across two client folders, named using a consistent file naming convention you decide on — state the convention in one sentence at the top of your folder.
Rename at least three badly-named files (e.g. IMG_0001.mp4) to follow your convention.
Take a screenshot of the full folder tree, expanded, so the structure is visible.
Write two sentences explaining how this structure and naming convention would help a new editor joining the agency find the right file quickly.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: I judge a naming convention by one test: can someone who's never seen this project find the right file in under ten seconds, just from the name? If the answer's no, the convention has failed regardless of how 'organised' it looks.

blocks.intro: Describe the purpose of data organisation for the videographer. (2 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark
cards.text: "To keep things tidy." Too general.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "So footage for each wedding can be found quickly and is not mixed up with another couple's files, saving editing time."

blocks.title: The graduation podcast
blocks.intro: A school is producing a podcast and a website for its Year 12 graduation.

steps.situation: Compare vector and raster for the graduation logo.

choices.text: A vector logo is made of shapes so it stays sharp at any size, while a raster logo is pixels and blurs when enlarged, but raster suits photos.
choices.feedback: Both types, with a difference and a link to use.

choices.text: They are the same.
choices.feedback: They differ in how they are made and scale.

choices.text: Raster is always better.
choices.feedback: Not for logos that must scale.

steps.situation: Pick an audio format to upload the podcast to the website.

choices.text: MP3, because it is compressed so the file is smaller and loads and downloads faster.
choices.feedback: A format and a reason.

choices.text: WAV, because it is the biggest.
choices.feedback: Large files slow the website.

choices.text: SVG.
choices.feedback: That is a graphics format.

blocks.title: Export One Logo, Three Formats
blocks.intro: Using the food truck logo scenario from this lesson, export the same source image in the formats that actually suit each use case, then compare the results.
steps: Create or find a simple logo design (text plus one shape is enough).
Export it as an SVG (or .ai/.eps if your software doesn't support SVG) — this is your scalable master.
Export the same logo as a PNG at 1000px wide, and again at 32px wide (favicon size).
Open both PNG exports and compare how the small one looks — note any blurring or loss of detail.
Resize the SVG (or vector file) to 32px in your software instead, and compare its sharpness to the small PNG.
Record a 15–30 second voice note (any audio app) and export it as both a WAV and an MP3. Compare the file sizes.
Write a short comparison: which format held up better at small size, and which audio format you'd upload to a podcast platform and why.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Vector for the logo, every time, when it has to scale — it's maths, not pixels, so a van wrap and a favicon come from the exact same file with zero quality loss. Raster locks you into the resolution you exported at, and someone always asks for it bigger later.

blocks.intro: Identify a suitable format for the logo and justify it. (2 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark
cards.text: "JPEG." — No reason, and JPEG does not scale or support transparency.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "SVG, because it is a vector format, so the logo stays sharp at any size, from a business card to the side of the truck."

items.why: Sample the hum and remove it.

items.text: The radio station needs an MP3, not a phone recording.

blocks.title: The 60-second radio ad
blocks.intro: A cafe owner records a 60-second radio ad on her phone. The radio station needs an MP3 file no longer than 30 seconds.

steps.situation: Which two editing features should she use?

choices.text: Trim and cut to shorten it to 30 seconds, and noise reduction to remove background sound from the phone recording.
choices.feedback: Two features, each linked to the problem.

choices.text: Add more music.
choices.feedback: That does not shorten it.

choices.text: Nothing, send it as is.
choices.feedback: It is too long.

steps.situation: Why must she export or convert it first?

choices.text: The phone saves in a different format, and the station needs an MP3, so she must export or convert it to that format.
choices.feedback: Format mismatch explained.

choices.text: Exporting makes it louder.
choices.feedback: Not the reason.

choices.text: It is not necessary.
choices.feedback: The station needs MP3.

blocks.title: Clean Up a Voiceover Recording
blocks.intro: Record a rough 30–60 second voiceover with a deliberate flaw — background noise, uneven volume, or an awkward pause — then fix it using real editing features, not just a re-record.
steps: Open Audacity and record yourself reading a short paragraph aloud, including at least one long pause and one moment where your voice gets quieter.
Use the Noise Reduction effect to remove any background hum or hiss.
Use the Normalize or Amplify effect so the volume is consistent throughout.
Select and delete the awkward pause using the Trim/cut tools, then listen back to check the cut is clean.
Add a simple fade-in at the start and fade-out at the end.
Export the finished file as an MP3 (File > Export > Export as MP3) — not the raw project file — so it's actually ready to send.
Write one sentence naming which two editing features made the biggest improvement.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Clients almost never flag 'the file won't open' as an editing problem, but it usually is one — sending a huge, uncompressed master file instead of exporting or converting it for delivery is the single most common reason a finished job gets stuck in someone's inbox.

cards.heading: Earns full marks

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Ignoring updates isn't a convenience trade-off, it's a security decision whether people realise it or not — most patches exist specifically to close a vulnerability that's already being exploited somewhere. 'I'll do it later' on an update is a risk decision, say it plainly.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Proprietary software usually buys guaranteed support and regular updates for a price; the free or open alternative buys flexibility and zero licence cost but often means the group is on their own when something breaks. blocks.title: Build the Sports Club Membership Sheet
blocks.intro: Build a working version of the membership sheet from this lesson, fixing the exact problem described — inconsistent number formats breaking the totals.
steps: Create a new sheet with a heading row: Member Name, Age, Membership Type, Price, Join Date.
Enter 10 rows of sample members. Deliberately enter at least two prices as text (e.g. with a leading space or as '$45' typed into a general-formatted cell) so you can see the problem.
In a new column, write a SUM formula over the Price column and confirm it gives the wrong total (or an error) because of the inconsistent entries.
Fix every cell in the Price column to use the same Currency number format, re-entering any that were stored as text.
Confirm the SUM formula now gives the correct total.
Apply a heading row style (bold, fill colour) and freeze the top row (View > Freeze > 1 row) so it stays visible when scrolling.
Add Conditional Formatting that highlights any membership priced above $50.
Save the file as lastname-membership-sheet.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: A heading row, one data type per column, and a consistent number format aren't style preferences — they're what makes formulas and sorting actually work. Mixed text and numbers in one 'price' column is the single most common reason a club treasurer's totals don't add up.

blocks.title: The surf school bookings
blocks.intro: A surf school has a spreadsheet of 500 bookings with columns for Name, Lesson date, Level (Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced) and Paid (Yes/No).

steps.situation: Describe a multi-level sort to organise the bookings.

choices.text: Sort by Lesson date first, then by Level within each date, so each day's bookings are grouped by level.
choices.feedback: Two levels, in order, with the effect.

choices.text: Delete half the rows.
choices.feedback: Sorting does not delete.

choices.text: Sort only by Paid.
choices.feedback: That is a single-level sort.

steps.situation: How could filters find beginners who have not paid, and what is a benefit?

choices.text: Filter Level = Beginner and Paid = No to show only those rows. The benefit is the data is only hidden, not deleted, so the owner can chase payments and then clear the filter.
choices.feedback: Two filters and a benefit.

choices.text: Sort by Name.
choices.feedback: Sorting does not select rows.

choices.text: Delete everyone else.
choices.feedback: Filters hide, they do not delete.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Sort rearranges everything permanently (until you sort again); filter temporarily hides rows that don't match, leaving the underlying data untouched. If the club needs to find a subgroup without disturbing the master list for everyone else, filter is always the right tool, not sort.

blocks.heading: Rory’s client brief
blocks.text: Bunbury Surf Club needs a 30-second Nippers sign-up reel in three weeks. The team has one phone, a free editing app and no budget. Could they add a 10-second ad without changing the deadline? Keep the four considerations in mind.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

blocks.title: Scope, time, resources and the brief

watchFor: What is in and out of scope

rows: What the project will and will not produce: the features, content and size of the final product.

blocks.title: Create a One-Page Plan for the Nippers Reel

steps: Title the document Nippers Sign-Up Reel: Project Plan.
Add a four-row table for Scope, Time, Resources and Client brief.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Design criteria that aren't testable are useless to a project manager — 'make it fun' can't be checked off at the end. 'Under 90 seconds, features at least three activities, suitable for ages 6 to 12' can actually be verified against the finished product.

blocks.title: Storyboard the Animated Safety Message
blocks.software: Any drawing tool, or pen and paper photographed/scanned
blocks.intro: Produce real thumbnails and a storyboard for the animated safety message from this lesson, with proper annotations — the planning artefact a client actually reviews before production starts.
steps: Sketch six quick thumbnails (simple boxes with rough shapes, no detail) showing the sequence of the safety message from start to finish.
Choose your strongest three thumbnails and redraw them as full storyboard frames with more detail.
Under each of the three frames, add two annotations: one about timing (how many seconds this frame lasts) and one about the transition into the next frame (cut, fade, wipe).
Add a short written note explaining what changed between your six rough thumbnails and your final three frames, and why.
Photograph or export your storyboard as a single document.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Thumbnails exist to let you fail fast and cheap — a bad sequence idea costs ten seconds to scrap on paper and hours to scrap once it's animated. Any team that skips straight to production because 'we know what we want' ends up redoing more work than they saved.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "A storyboard shows each scene in order with timing and audio notes, so the client can check the sequence and message before any animation time is spent."

blocks.title: Evaluate a Real Digital Product
blocks.intro: Evaluate an actual website or app you use regularly — like the school canteen ordering page from this lesson — against real criteria and real evidence, not opinion.
steps: Choose a real website or app you use at least weekly.
Write three testable design criteria it should meet (e.g. 'loads in under 3 seconds on mobile data', 'checkout completes in 4 taps or fewer').
Gather actual evidence for each criterion: a timed screen recording, a step count, or a short survey of two other users.
For each criterion, state clearly whether the product met it, using your evidence, not a guess.
Write a one-paragraph self-reflection on how the evidence-gathering changed your opinion of the product compared to your first impression.
Recommend one specific, actionable change based on your evaluation.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Self-reflection without evidence is just an opinion with extra steps. 'I think it worked well' earns nothing from a marker or a client — a screenshot of actual usage, a user comment, a measured outcome is what turns an opinion into an evaluation.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "Criterion: order in 4 taps or fewer. Not met: testers took 6 taps. Adding a Quick order button would reduce this to 3."

blocks.heading: 🎟️ TICKET
blocks.text: A real estate agent's 24 MB house photo is killing their website's load time, and the same file needs to go to print, online and email — three completely different jobs from one source image. File optimisation isn't one setting, it's choosing the right resolution, colour mode and format for where the file actually ends up.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

cards.heading: Explain the purpose of file optimisation.
Compare optimisation for print and for online use.
Choose settings for a given environment.

blocks.title: One photo, three destinations
blocks.brief: A short screen recording exporting one 24 MB photo for print, for a website and for email, showing the size and pixel dimensions each time. Suggested source: a teacher-filmed demo in Photopea or Canva.
watchFor: How fast pages load with small files

items.definition: Adjusting a file's size, resolution, format and colour so it suits where it will be used, with the smallest size that still looks right.
Detail in an image. Print is measured in pixels per inch (ppi); screens use pixel dimensions (e.g. 1920 x 1080).
Needs high resolution (about 300 ppi) and CMYK colour, so files are large.
Needs small files sized in pixels for the screen, in RGB colour, so pages load quickly.
Files used on devices but not the web, e.g. a presentation or interactive PDF. Balance quality and size.

blocks.title: The 18 MB team photo
blocks.intro: A school uses the same 18 MB photo of its sports team on its website home page and in a printed yearbook.

steps.situation: The home page is slow to load.

choices.text: The 18 MB file is far larger than a screen needs, so it takes a long time to download, especially on phones.
choices.feedback: It links the file size to the loading time.

choices.text: The photo is the wrong colour.
choices.feedback: Colour does not cause slow loading.

choices.text: Websites cannot show photos.
choices.feedback: They can, if the file is optimised.

steps.situation: The school optimises the photo for both uses.

choices.text: Website: resize to a screen size in RGB as a small JPEG. Yearbook: keep about 300 ppi at the printed size in CMYK.
choices.feedback: Each use gets its own settings.

choices.text: Use the same 18 MB file for both.
choices.feedback: That is the problem, not the fix.

choices.text: Shrink the yearbook photo to 300 KB.

blocks.title: Optimise One Photo, Three Ways
blocks.software: Any photo editor (Photoshop, GIMP, Photopea, or your phone's editor)
blocks.intro: Take the real estate photo scenario from this lesson and actually produce the three optimised versions it needs.
steps: Find or take one photo at least 3000px wide.
Export a print version: resize so the longest edge is sized for a printed A4 page at 300 ppi, and if your software supports it, convert to CMYK.
Export a website version: resize to 1600px wide, save as JPEG, and check the file size is under 500KB.
Export an email version: resize to 1200px wide and check it would fit within a typical 10MB email attachment limit alongside other files.
Open all three exports and compare their file sizes in a table.
Write one sentence explaining why the print version is allowed to be so much larger than the other two.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SLOANE VANE
blocks.text: Nobody ever gets marked down for knowing print needs 300 ppi — they get marked down for not explaining why online doesn't. Say it out loud: screens display pixels, not printed dots, so 'resolution' for online is about pixel dimensions fitting the screen, not ppi at all.

cards.front: What is file optimisation?
cards.back: Adjusting a file's size, resolution, format and colour so it suits where it will be used, with the smallest size that still looks good.

cards.front: How does optimising for print differ from online?
cards.back: Print needs about 300 ppi and CMYK so files are large. Online needs small RGB files sized in pixels so pages load quickly.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
