blocks.heading: 🎟️ TICKET
blocks.text: Two files, two very different compression needs crossed my desk this week — and picking the wrong type for the wrong job either wrecks the quality or barely shrinks the file. Compression isn't a single technique; justifying lossy versus lossless for a specific use is exactly what gets tested.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

cards.heading: Select a compression type for a file and justify it.

blocks.title: Lossy or lossless?
blocks.brief: A short clip comparing a photo saved as high and low quality JPEG and as PNG, then zipping a folder to show nothing is lost. Suggested source: a teacher-filmed screen recording.
watchFor: What is thrown away in lossy compression
Why logos and text suit lossless
How much smaller each option is

rows: Reducing file size so data transfers faster and uses less storage.
Permanently removes some data the user is unlikely to notice. Much smaller files; quality can drop.
Reduces size without losing any data; the original can be restored exactly.
How much storage a file uses: KB, MB, GB.

blocks.title: Lossy vs lossless
blocks.alt: Two panels comparing lossy compression, which discards data, with lossless, which keeps every bit.

blocks.title: File size lab: JPEG against PNG
Which compression fits?
blocks.instruction: A designer is sending four files. Tap the best type.

items.text: Holiday photos for Instagram.
items.why: Quality loss is not noticed on a phone, and files stay small.

items.text: The client's logo with text.

items.why: Every character must be exactly the same.

items.text: Music for streaming.
12 songs sent to a record label for mastering.

items.why: Smaller files download faster and quality loss is acceptable.

blocks.title: The band's two uses
blocks.intro: A band is sending 12 songs to a record label for mastering, and 12 songs to fans as a free download.

steps.situation: The label will master the tracks.
steps.prompt: Which compression should the band use?

choices.text: Lossless, because mastering needs every detail of the original recording.
choices.feedback: It names the type and justifies it with the use.

choices.text: Lossy, because it is smaller.
choices.feedback: Size is not the priority when the label needs full quality.

choices.text: No compression is possible.
choices.feedback: Lossless compression keeps quality.

steps.situation: The fans download the songs.

choices.text: Lossy, because smaller files download faster and the quality loss is acceptable for listening.
choices.feedback: It justifies lossy with the use.

choices.text: Lossless, because it is always better.
choices.feedback: Not always. Large files slow the download.

choices.text: Neither.
choices.feedback: Compression helps both uses.

blocks.title: Match the feature to lossy compression
blocks.instruction: Tap a feature on the left, then tap what's true of it under lossy compression.

right: Yes, permanently
Much smaller
Can drop, especially if saved repeatedly
Small size matters more than perfect quality

links: Can drop, especially if saved repeatedly
Small size matters more than perfect quality

blocks.explanation: Lossy compression trades some quality away permanently in exchange for a much smaller file.

blocks.title: Compare Lossy and Lossless Compression
blocks.software: Any file archiver (7-Zip, WinZip, or your OS's built-in zip) and a photo editor
blocks.intro: Compress the same content two different ways and see the actual size and quality trade-off, instead of just reading about it.
steps: Take a photo (JPEG) and a text document of similar visual complexity.
Save the photo as a JPEG at two different quality settings (e.g. 90% and 40%) and compare the file sizes and visible quality loss — this is lossy compression.
Zip the text document using your OS's built-in compression and compare the zipped size to the original — this is lossless; unzip it and confirm it's identical to the original, with nothing lost.
Try zipping the already-compressed JPEG and note how little smaller it gets — lossy formats are already compressed, so there's little left to save.
Write a one-paragraph justification: which type of compression you'd use for the two scenarios in this lesson's quiz, and why.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SLOANE VANE
blocks.text: My rule of thumb: if the file needs to be restored byte-for-byte identical — a document, a database export — it's lossless, no exceptions. If it's a photo or audio where a human eye or ear won't notice the difference, lossy buys you a much smaller file for free.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Compare lossy and lossless compression. (4 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark
cards.text: "Lossy loses quality. Lossless does not." One feature only; no examples.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "Lossy permanently removes data, so files like JPEG are much smaller but lower quality; lossless keeps all the data, so PNG or ZIP files can be restored exactly but are larger."

cards.heading: Scenario
cards.text: A band is sending 12 songs to a record label for mastering, and 12 songs to fans as a free download. Answer the questions below using this scenario.

question.text: State the purpose of compression.
question.explanation: 1 mark – Reduces file size for faster transfer and less storage

question.text: Justify a type of compression for each of the two uses.

cards.heading: Know the purpose
cards.text: Compression reduces file size so files store and send faster.

cards.heading: Justify the type
cards.text: Lossless when exactness matters, lossy when small size matters more.

cards.heading: Aim for
cards.text: At least 4/5 on the practice questions. If not, reread the table and test tip.

blocks.heading: 🎟️ TICKET
blocks.text: A website photo needs cropping to fit a banner, and a PDF is bloated because nobody resampled the images inside it before export. Cropping and resampling get confused constantly — one changes what's in the frame, the other changes how much data describes it.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

cards.heading: Explain how each reduces file size.
Apply both to prepare an image for a product.

blocks.title: Crop first, then resample
blocks.brief: A short screen recording cropping a photo, downsampling it to its display size and exporting it, with the file size shown at each step. Suggested source: a teacher-filmed demo in Photopea.
watchFor: Pixels before and after each step

items.definition: Removing unwanted areas from the edges of an image. Fewer pixels, smaller file, and a stronger composition.
Changing the number of pixels in an image. Downsampling reduces the pixel dimensions and file size.
Width x height in pixels, e.g. 6000 x 4000.
Adding pixels. Makes the file larger and the image blurry; avoid it.

blocks.title: Put the workflow in order
blocks.instruction: Tap the four steps in order.
items: Keep the original and work on a copy.
Crop first to remove what you do not need.
Resample down to the size it will display at.
Export, choosing the format and quality.
blocks.explanation: Crop, then resample, on a copy. Resampling down cannot be undone.

blocks.title: File size lab: crop and resample
Cropping or resampling?
blocks.instruction: Which operation does each statement describe?

items.text: Removes unwanted areas from the edges.
Changes the number of pixels in the image.
Can strengthen the composition, for example moving the subject onto a thirds line.
items.why: Cropping changes what is in the frame.

items.text: Downsampling reduces the pixel dimensions and file size.
items.why: Fewer pixels mean a smaller file.

items.text: Upsampling adds pixels and makes the image blurry, so avoid it.

blocks.title: The 80 MB PDF
blocks.intro: A student places a 5 MB photo of a school building in an interactive PDF, where it only fills a small box 600 pixels wide. The PDF is now 80 MB.

steps.situation: She wants to shrink the PDF.

choices.text: Downsample the photo to about 600 pixels wide before placing it, so each copy is a small file.
choices.feedback: Resampling to the display size cuts the size dramatically.

choices.text: Upsample the photo.
choices.feedback: That makes the file larger and blurrier.

choices.text: Rename the file.
choices.feedback: Names do not change size.

blocks.title: Crop and Resample a Website Photo
blocks.intro: Apply cropping and resampling as two separate, distinct operations on the same photo, so the difference between them is obvious in your own result.
steps: Open a photo at least 3000px wide.
Crop it to a 16:9 banner shape, removing unwanted parts of the frame — note the new pixel dimensions after cropping.
Save this cropped version as Version-A.
Starting again from the cropped version, resample it down to 1200px wide without cropping anything further — the framing stays the same, only the pixel count changes.
Save this as Version-B and compare its file size to Version-A.
Zoom in to 200% on both versions and compare sharpness.
Write two sentences explaining, in your own result, what cropping changed versus what resampling changed.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SLOANE VANE
blocks.text: Cropping removes part of the image — the pixel dimensions and framing both change. Resampling reduces the number of pixels describing the same framing — the content stays, the detail shrinks. Confuse the two in an answer and I know immediately the concept isn't understood, just the word.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Describe how resampling reduces file size. (2 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark
cards.text: "It makes the picture smaller." Does not mention pixels.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "Resampling reduces the number of pixels, e.g. from 6000 wide to 1200 wide, so there is much less data to store."

cards.heading: Scenario
cards.text: A student places a 5 MB photo of a school building in an interactive PDF, where it only fills a small box 600 pixels wide. The PDF is now 80 MB. Answer the questions below using this scenario.

question.text: Describe how cropping could be used on the photo.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Describes removing unneeded areas around the building so fewer pixels are stored and the building is the focus
1 mark – States that it cuts part of the image

question.text: Explain how resampling would reduce the size of the PDF.
question.explanation:
3 marks – Explains downsampling the photo to about 600 pixels wide removes pixels the box cannot display, greatly reducing each image and the total PDF size
2 marks – Describes reducing pixels
1 mark – States it makes the image smaller

cards.heading: Crop then resample
cards.text: Crop first, then reduce to the display size, always on a copy.

cards.heading: Avoid upsampling
cards.text: It adds pixels but no detail, so the image looks blurry.

cards.heading: Aim for
cards.text: At least 4/5 on the practice questions.

blocks.heading: 🎟️ TICKET
blocks.text: A netball club's shared files are a mess — someone's working copy got overwritten, nobody can find last season's roster. Shared folders, permissions, sync, search and tags — this is the unglamorous admin work that determines whether a volunteer-run club's data survives contact with real life.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

cards.heading: Describe strategies for managing data online.
Explain the benefit of each strategy.
Apply strategies to a shared project folder.

blocks.brief: A short walk-through of a shared OneDrive folder for a club: subfolders, file names, permissions and an archive. Suggested source: a teacher-filmed screen recording using a school OneDrive.

items.definition: Organising, storing, sharing and protecting files kept online (e.g. OneDrive, Google Drive).
An online folder that set people can open, with chosen permissions.
Who can view, comment or edit a file or folder.
Keeping the same files up to date on the cloud and on each device.
Finding files by name, content or labels instead of browsing.

blocks.title: Good or poor practice?
blocks.instruction: Four students share a Google Drive folder. Is each habit good or poor?

items.text: Files named doc1, final and final2.
items.why: Names should describe the content and date.

items.text: Fixtures_Round03_2027-05-10.pdf
items.why: A consistent name with a date sorts in order.

items.text: Everyone has edit access to every file.
items.why: Anyone can delete someone else's work.

items.text: The treasurer can edit Finance while coaches only view it.
items.why: Permissions match what each person needs.

items.text: Last season's files moved to an Archive folder.
items.why: It keeps the live folder tidy.

items.text: Leaving access on after a member leaves.
items.why: Access should be removed when people leave.

blocks.title: The deleted work
blocks.intro: Four students share a Google Drive folder. One accidentally deleted another's work.

steps.situation: How could permissions have prevented it?

choices.text: Give each student edit access only to their own section and view access to the rest, so they cannot delete each other's work.
choices.feedback: It links permissions to the problem.

choices.text: Give everyone edit access to everything.
choices.feedback: That caused the problem.

choices.text: Tell people to be careful.
choices.feedback: A request is not a control.

blocks.title: Check your understanding
blocks.instruction: Answer first, then flip.

cards.front: What are permissions?
cards.back: Who can view, comment or edit a file or folder.

cards.front: What does sync do?
cards.back: Keeps the same files up to date on the cloud and on each device.

cards.front: Name two ways to share and protect files.
cards.back: Any two of: share links with the least permission needed, remove access when people leave, turn on two-step verification, check sync before working offline.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SLOANE VANE
blocks.text: Most 'someone deleted my file' disasters are actually a permissions failure, not malice — give everyone full edit access to everything and eventually someone will overwrite or delete work they didn't mean to touch. Tiered permissions aren't bureaucracy, they're damage control.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Describe one strategy for efficient online data management. (2 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark
cards.text: "Use OneDrive." A product, not a strategy.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "Give coaches view-only permission on the Finance folder, so they can see the budget but cannot change it by accident."

cards.heading: Scenario
cards.text: Four students share a Google Drive folder for a group project. Files are called "doc1", "final", "final2", and one student accidentally deleted another's work. Answer the questions below using this scenario.

question.text: Describe two strategies that would make the group's online data management more efficient.
Explain how permissions could have prevented the deleted work.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Explains giving each student edit rights only to their own files (others view or comment), so they cannot delete them
1 mark – States permissions control access

cards.heading: Structure and naming
cards.text: Logical folders and consistent file names.

cards.heading: Protect with permissions
cards.text: Least access needed, removed when people leave.

cards.heading: Aim for
cards.text: At least 5/6 on the practice questions.

blocks.heading: 🎟️ TICKET
blocks.text: A club newsletter went through six 'final' versions and nobody can find which one actually got sent. Version control — numbering, history, a master copy, checking files out — exists entirely to prevent this exact chaos, and it's cheap insurance most small teams skip until it bites them.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

cards.heading: Apply a version naming convention and use version history.

blocks.title: Version history in action
blocks.brief: A short clip restoring yesterday's version of a document from version history and showing a v01, v02 naming pattern. Suggested source: a teacher-filmed recording in Word online or Google Docs.

items.definition: Managing changes to a document so the current version is clear and earlier versions can be found or restored.
Adding v01, v02 to file names; major changes can use v1.0, v2.0.
A record kept by OneDrive or Google Docs of every saved version, which can be viewed or restored.
The single, official current version of a document.
Locking a file while one person edits it, so others cannot overwrite changes.

blocks.title: Bad against good
blocks.alt: Two panels: emailed copies with confusing names, and one shared master with numbered versions.

blocks.title: Bad or good version control?
blocks.instruction: Sort each habit.

items.text: Emailing yourself Essay, Essay new and Essay latest.
items.why: You cannot tell which copy has the feedback.

items.text: Saving copies as Report_v01 and Report_v02.
Keeping one master copy in a shared folder.
Report_final_REAL.docx
items.why: Names like this say nothing about order.

items.text: Restoring yesterday's version from version history.
items.why: History lets you recover from mistakes.

blocks.title: 14 copies of an essay
blocks.intro: A student emails her draft essay to herself each night. She now has 14 copies called Essay, Essay new and Essay latest and cannot tell which has her teacher's feedback.

steps.situation: She asks how to fix this.

choices.text: Keep one master copy in a shared folder, number saved versions (v01, v02) and use version history to restore earlier work.
choices.feedback: Numbering and a single master with history solve it.

choices.text: Email herself more often.
choices.feedback: More copies makes it worse.

choices.text: Delete all but the newest.
choices.feedback: She cannot tell which is newest or has the feedback.

blocks.title: Check your understanding
blocks.instruction: Answer first, then flip.

cards.front: What is document version control?
cards.back: Managing changes to a document so the current version is clear and earlier versions can be found or restored.

cards.front: What is a master copy?
cards.back: The single, official current version of a document.

cards.front: What does check out do?
cards.back: Locks a file while one person edits it, so others cannot overwrite changes.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SLOANE VANE
blocks.text: A file literally named 'final_FINAL_v2_useThisOne.docx' is the single clearest sign version control has already failed. If your naming convention needs an adjective to tell people which one's current, the system is broken, not the file.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Explain how version history supports version control. (2 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark
cards.text: "It saves versions." Repeats the term.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "It keeps a record of every saved version with the date and editor, so if work is overwritten, an earlier version can be restored."

cards.heading: Scenario
cards.text: A student emails her draft essay to herself each night. She now has 14 copies called "Essay", "Essay new", "Essay latest" and cannot tell which has her teacher's feedback. Answer the questions below using this scenario.

question.text: Define document version control.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Defines managing changes so the current version is clear and earlier versions can be retrieved
1 mark – States it is saving versions

question.text: Describe two version control strategies the student should use.

cards.heading: One master copy
cards.text: Never email attachments around.

cards.heading: Number and date versions
cards.text: v01, v02 and YYYY-MM-DD, with a change note.

cards.heading: Aim for
cards.text: At least 4/6 on the practice questions.

blocks.text: Next lesson: the concept of cloud computing.

blocks.heading: 🎟️ TICKET
blocks.text: A mobile hairdresser wants to ditch the laptop she drags between appointments and run everything from her phone instead. Cloud computing's real sell for someone like her isn't the buzzword — it's that her bookings and client notes follow her, with trade-offs she needs to understand before she commits.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

cards.heading: Explain the concept of cloud computing.
Explain advantages and disadvantages for a user.

blocks.title: What is the cloud?
blocks.brief: A short clip showing files, bookings and accounting software used from a tablet and a phone with nothing stored locally. Suggested source: a teacher-filmed demonstration with a cloud booking app and OneDrive.

Saving files on the provider's servers.
Applications used through a browser or app, paid by subscription.
Servers and tools rented to run websites and apps.

blocks.title: Advantage or disadvantage?
blocks.instruction: Sort each effect of cloud computing.

items.text: Access from any device, anywhere.
Needs a reliable internet connection.
Automatic backup by the provider.
Ongoing subscription cost.
No expensive servers to buy.
Data held by a third party, sometimes overseas.
items.why: The user has less control over it.

items.text: Storage can grow as needed.
A provider outage stops work.
items.why: The user depends on the provider being up.

blocks.title: The accounting firm
blocks.intro: A small accounting firm is deciding whether to replace its office server with cloud storage and cloud accounting software.

steps.situation: The partner asks for one real advantage.

choices.text: Staff can open client files from any device at any site, and the provider backs them up automatically.
choices.feedback: A real advantage linked to the firm.

choices.text: The cloud is modern.
choices.feedback: Not an advantage and not linked to the firm.

choices.text: It is always free.
choices.feedback: There is an ongoing subscription.

steps.situation: She asks for one real disadvantage.

choices.text: If the internet or the provider goes down, staff cannot reach client files, and the data sits with a third party.
choices.feedback: It links the downside to the firm's work.

choices.text: The cloud has no disadvantages.
choices.feedback: There are several.

choices.text: It uses too much power at the office.
choices.feedback: The provider runs the servers, not the firm.

blocks.title: Check your understanding
blocks.instruction: Answer first, then flip.

cards.front: What is cloud computing?
cards.back: Using storage and software on a provider's servers over the internet instead of on your own equipment.

cards.front: Why did the stolen tablet lose nothing?
cards.back: The files were synced to the cloud, so she logs in on a new device.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SLOANE VANE
blocks.text: I always make clients name one real advantage and one real disadvantage before signing off on a cloud move — not just the sales pitch. Access-anywhere is genuinely powerful for a mobile worker; losing it the moment her connection drops is the cost nobody mentions upfront.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Explain the concept of cloud computing. (2 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark
cards.text: "Saving to the cloud." — Uses the term to explain itself.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "Data and software are stored on remote servers owned by a provider and accessed over the internet, instead of on the user's own computer."

cards.text: A small accounting firm is deciding whether to replace its office server with cloud storage and cloud accounting software. Answer the questions below using this scenario.

question.text: Explain the concept of cloud computing.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Explains data and software on remote servers accessed over the internet
1 mark – States files are stored online

question.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of cloud computing for the firm.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Advantage explained with a link to the firm (e.g. staff can work from home or client offices)
2 marks – Disadvantage explained with a link to the firm (e.g. client financial data is held by a third party; no access if the internet fails)

cards.heading: Define it
cards.text: Storage and software on a provider's servers, used over the internet.

cards.heading: Give both sides
cards.text: A real advantage and a real disadvantage, linked to the business.

blocks.heading: 🎟️ TICKET
blocks.text: A family laptop's crawling and everyone assumes it needs replacing. Nine times out of ten it just needs the maintenance it's never had — disk clean-up, clearing the internet cache, checking temporary files — before anyone spends money on new hardware.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

cards.heading: Describe disk clean-up, temporary file and cache deletion, and defragmentation.
Identify when defragmentation should not be used.

blocks.title: Keeping a computer healthy
blocks.brief: A short clip running Disk Clean-up, clearing the browser cache and checking whether a drive is an HDD or an SSD. Suggested source: a teacher-filmed screen recording on a school laptop.
watchFor: How much space a clean-up frees
Why the cache can fix a website

items.definition: Software that maintains or protects the computer rather than doing a user task.
Finds and removes unneeded files (temporary files, recycle bin, old updates) to free storage space.
Files programs create while working; many are left behind and waste space.
Copies of web pages and images saved by the browser so sites load faster. Clearing it frees space and can fix display errors.
Parts of a file are scattered across a hard disk drive, so it takes longer to read. Defragmentation rearranges them. Not needed on SSDs; Windows optimises SSDs differently.

blocks.title: Why defragmenting depends on the drive
blocks.alt: Two panels: a hard disk drive scatters file parts so defragmenting helps, and an SSD has no moving parts so defragmenting is not needed.

Files slow to open on an old HDD

blocks.title: Which tool fixes it?
blocks.instruction: A 6-year-old desktop with a hard disk drive is slow. Tap the tool.

items.text: Only 2 GB free, mostly old update files and temporary files.
items.why: Disk clean-up removes unneeded files to free space.

items.text: A website keeps showing old images.
items.why: Clearing the cache removes the saved copies.

items.text: The HDD is 30% fragmented and files open slowly.
The recycle bin and temporary files are using 18 GB.
items.why: Clean-up removes recycle bin and temporary files.

items.text: The browser has not been cleared for two years.

blocks.title: The 95% full laptop
blocks.intro: A student's laptop has an SSD that is 95% full. Her browser has not been cleared for two years.

steps.situation: She asks which two utilities would help.

choices.text: Disk clean-up to remove temporary files and free storage, and clearing the browser cache to free space and remove old saved pages.
choices.feedback: Both target the space problem.

choices.text: Defragmentation and a spam filter.
choices.feedback: Defragmentation is not for SSDs, and a spam filter is not a maintenance utility here.

choices.text: Buy a new laptop.
choices.feedback: Not a utility tool.

steps.situation: She wonders about defragmenting.
steps.prompt: Why is it not needed on her laptop?

choices.text: An SSD has no moving parts, so scattered file parts do not slow it, and defragmenting would add wear.
choices.feedback: It names the drive type and the reason.

choices.text: Laptops cannot be defragmented.
choices.feedback: Not the reason.

choices.text: The laptop is too full.
choices.feedback: Fullness is not why.

blocks.title: Run a Real Maintenance Check
blocks.intro: Actually run the maintenance utilities from this lesson on a real computer and report genuine findings — not hypothetical ones.
steps: On Windows, open Disk Cleanup (search for it in the Start menu) or on Mac, open About This Mac > Storage > Manage. Record how much space it reports could be freed.
Check your browser's cache size (in browser settings, under Privacy) and clear it, noting the space freed.
Check your Downloads and Temp folders for old files you no longer need — note how many and their total size.
Check whether your main drive is an SSD or a traditional HDD (Settings > System > Storage > Disk, or About This Mac). Record which it is.
If it's an SSD, do not run defragmentation — instead explain in one sentence why it isn't needed. If it's an HDD, you may run defragmentation and note how long it takes.
Write a short summary of what you found and freed, as if reporting back to the family from this lesson's scenario.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SLOANE VANE
blocks.text: Defragmentation is the classic trap question — it's essential on an old spinning hard drive and actively unnecessary, even mildly harmful, on an SSD, which have no moving parts to benefit from it. If a laptop has an SSD, say so and explain why defrag doesn't apply.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Explain how defragmentation improves performance. (2 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark
cards.text: "It cleans the disk." That is disk clean-up.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "It moves the scattered parts of each file together on the hard disk drive, so the drive reads files in one pass and they open faster."

cards.heading: Scenario
cards.text: A student's laptop has an SSD that is 95% full. Her browser has not been cleared for two years. Answer the questions below using this scenario.

question.text: Describe how two utility tools could help the laptop.
Explain why defragmentation is not needed on her laptop.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Explains SSDs have no moving parts and access all locations equally fast, so fragmentation does not slow them
1 mark – States it is an SSD

cards.heading: Name the tool and what it does
cards.text: Clean-up frees space, cache clearing frees space, defrag rearranges an HDD.

cards.heading: Check the drive
cards.text: No defragmentation on an SSD.

cards.heading: Aim for
cards.text: At least 5/6 on the practice questions.

blocks.heading: 🎟️ TICKET
blocks.text: A suspicious email just hit a family's inbox and something's already behaving strangely on their laptop. Malware, virus, spyware, anti-virus, spam filters — identifying exactly what kind of threat you're dealing with changes what protection actually stops it.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

cards.heading: Describe the purpose of anti-malware, anti-virus and spam filters.

blocks.title: Malware and how to stop it
blocks.brief: A short clip showing a phishing email, the spam filter catching it, and anti-malware quarantining a bad attachment. Suggested source: a teacher-filmed screen recording using a safe demo, or an Australian Cyber Security Centre education video.
watchFor: The warning signs in the email

items.definition: Any software designed to harm a computer or steal data. Includes viruses, spyware, ransomware and trojans.
Malware that attaches to files and spreads when they are opened or shared.
Malware that secretly collects information such as passwords, browsing and keystrokes.
Scans files and memory, detects known threats and quarantines or removes them. Needs regular updates.
Moves unwanted or suspicious email to a junk folder, reducing phishing and malware links.

blocks.alt: Four steps: spam filter, if opened spyware, anti-malware scans, user action.

blocks.title: Tool or habit?
blocks.instruction: Sort each protection.

items.text: Anti-malware with real-time scanning.
Do not open unexpected attachments.
A spam filter in the email service.
Hover over links to check the address.
items.why: A behaviour that spots fake links.

items.text: Firewall turned on.
Use strong, different passwords.
Automatic updates.
items.why: A setting that installs security fixes.

items.text: Download software only from official sites.
items.why: A habit that avoids fake installers.

blocks.title: The slow family laptop
blocks.intro: A family laptop has become slow, shows pop-up ads, and a parent's bank password was used by someone else.

steps.situation: Which malware is most likely involved?

choices.text: Spyware: it secretly collects information such as passwords and browsing, which explains the stolen bank password.
choices.feedback: It names the type, what it does and links it to the evidence.

choices.text: A spam filter.
choices.feedback: That is a protection, not malware.

choices.text: A firewall.
choices.feedback: That is a protection, not malware.

steps.situation: How should the family protect the laptop?

choices.text: Run anti-malware with real-time scanning and turn on automatic updates, and avoid unexpected attachments and unofficial downloads.
choices.feedback: A tool and a habit, both tied to the problem.

choices.text: Turn the laptop off permanently.
choices.feedback: It does not protect the laptop in use.

choices.text: Share the password with the whole family.
choices.feedback: That makes it less secure.

blocks.title: Check your understanding
blocks.instruction: Answer first, then flip.

cards.front: What is malware?
cards.back: Any software designed to harm a computer or steal data, including viruses, spyware, ransomware and trojans.

cards.front: How is a virus different from spyware?
cards.back: A virus attaches to files and spreads when they are opened or shared. Spyware secretly collects information such as passwords.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SLOANE VANE
blocks.text: A virus and spyware aren't the same threat even though people lump them together — a virus spreads and disrupts, spyware quietly watches and steals information without the user noticing anything's wrong at all. Misname the malware type and your recommended fix won't match the actual problem.

blocks.intro: Describe the purpose of a spam filter. (2 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark
cards.text: "Spam is junk mail." — Describes the threat, not the tool.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "A spam filter checks incoming email and moves unwanted or suspicious messages to a junk folder, so users are less likely to open phishing links."

question.text: Describe two ways the family could protect the laptop.

blocks.heading: 🔧 JOB TICKET
blocks.text: A client's setting up a home office and asking why they'd bother networking two computers at all. Before you can design anything, you need the basics solid: what a network actually is, LAN versus WAN, and what 'shared resources' really buys someone.

cards.heading: Explain the concept and purpose of a computer network.

items.definition: Two or more devices connected so they can share data and resources.
A network in one building or site, e.g. a home, school or office.
A network over a large area. The internet is the largest WAN.
Hardware, software, files and an internet connection used by many devices on the network.

blocks.title: Packet Journey
blocks.caption: See a network in action before you work through the home network example.

pauseQuestions.question: Why is the message split into packets instead of being sent in one piece?
pauseQuestions.answer: Small packets share the network fairly, can take different routes, and if one is lost only that packet has to be sent again.

pauseQuestions.question: What is the job of the switch?
pauseQuestions.answer: It connects the devices inside one local network (LAN) and sends each packet to the right device.

pauseQuestions.question: What does the router do that the switch does not?
pauseQuestions.answer: It connects different networks, such as the school network and the internet. It reads each packet's destination address to decide where to send it.

pauseQuestions.question: Why do the packets arrive in the order 3, 1, 4, 2?
pauseQuestions.answer: Each packet can take a different route. Some routes are shorter or less busy, so the packets arrive out of order.

pauseQuestions.question: How does Sam's laptop rebuild the message in the right order?
pauseQuestions.answer: Every packet is numbered, so the laptop puts them back in number order.

pauseQuestions.question: What happens if one packet never arrives?
pauseQuestions.answer: Sam's laptop never confirms it, so your laptop sends that packet again.

blocks.title: Sort the effects of networking
blocks.instruction: Is each effect an advantage or a disadvantage of networking an office?

items.text: All staff print to one network printer instead of buying five.
Malware on one computer can spread to every device.
items.why: Connected devices can pass malware between them.

items.text: Files move between computers without USB drives.
items.why: Sharing files over the network saves time.

items.text: If the router fails, nobody has internet.
items.why: One shared connection is a single point of failure.

items.text: Everyone shares one internet connection.
items.why: One connection and bill instead of four.

items.text: Setting up and maintaining it costs money and skill.
items.why: A network needs set-up and ongoing maintenance.

blocks.title: Check your understanding
blocks.instruction: Answer first, then flip.

cards.front: What is a computer network?
cards.back: Two or more devices connected so they can share data and resources.

cards.front: LAN or WAN: which is the internet?
cards.back: WAN. A LAN covers one building or site, while the internet is the largest WAN.

cards.front: Why is 'you can share stuff' a weak answer?
cards.back: It is too vague. Name what is shared, such as one network printer for all staff.

blocks.title: The real estate office
blocks.intro: A real estate office has four computers, each with its own printer and internet connection. Staff move files between computers on USB drives.

steps.situation: The owner asks why they should network the computers.
steps.prompt: Which answer states the purpose best?

choices.text: A network connects the computers so they can share files, printers and one internet connection.
choices.feedback: It names what is shared, which is the purpose of the network.

choices.text: Networks are faster.
choices.feedback: Speed is not the purpose, and the answer names nothing shared.

choices.text: Everyone does it.
choices.feedback: Not a reason, and not linked to the office.

steps.situation: The owner asks about a downside.
steps.prompt: Which disadvantage is specific to this office?

choices.text: Security risk: any staff computer with malware could spread it to client files on the others.
choices.feedback: It names a real disadvantage and links it to the office's data.

choices.text: It costs money.
choices.feedback: A throwaway line. Say what it costs and why it matters here.

choices.text: There are no disadvantages.
choices.feedback: Every network has risks, such as malware spreading and a failed router.

blocks.heading: Sparky's point
blocks.text: When a client asks 'why network it', the honest answer is almost always sharing a printer, sharing files or sharing an internet connection. If your explanation does not land on one of those practical benefits, it is too abstract to convince anyone to pay for the job.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Describe one advantage of networking for a small office. (2 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark: "You can share stuff."
cards.text: Too vague.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "All staff can print to one network printer, so the office buys one printer instead of five." A named resource and the effect.

cards.heading: Scenario: The real estate office
cards.text: A real estate office has four computers, each with its own printer and internet connection. Staff move files between computers on USB drives. Answer the questions below using this scenario.

question.text: Explain the purpose of a computer network for the office.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Explains a network connects the computers so they can share files, printers and one internet connection
1 mark – States it connects computers

question.text: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of networking the office.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Advantage described with a link to the office
2 marks – Disadvantage described with a link to the office

cards.heading: Name what is shared
cards.text: Files, printers and an internet connection, tied to the office in the question.

cards.heading: Be specific on the downside
cards.text: Malware spreading or a single router failure, not just 'it costs money'.

cards.heading: Aim for
cards.text: At least 5/6 on the practice questions. If not, reread the key terms and test tip.

blocks.heading: 🔧 JOB TICKET
blocks.text: A client wants their shed connected to the house network and is asking whether wifi will just reach. Depends entirely on the medium — optic fibre, twisted pair, wireless — and each one has a job it's genuinely good at and a job it'll fail at. I've seen too many wireless-only sheds with constant dropouts.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

cards.heading: Describe optic fibre, wired and wireless media.
Compare transmission media on speed, distance, interference and mobility.
Select media for a location in a network.

blocks.title: Fibre, Ethernet and Wi-Fi
blocks.brief: A short clip showing each medium in the real world: a fibre run between buildings, an Ethernet patch panel and a wireless access point, with a note on where each fits. Suggested source: a teacher-filmed tour of the school's network room or a short cabling explainer.

items.definition: The physical path data travels along between devices.
Glass or plastic strands carrying data as pulses of light. Very fast, long distances, no electrical interference.
Copper Ethernet cable (e.g. Cat6) carrying electrical signals. Fast and reliable, up to about 100 m.
Radio waves (Wi-Fi). Devices can move around, but walls, distance and other devices reduce speed.

blocks.title: Match the medium to the place
blocks.instruction: A school uses each medium where it fits best. Tap the best medium.

items.text: From the street to the school and between buildings.
items.why: Long distance and very high speed.

items.text: Desktop computers in the library and the servers.
items.why: Fast, reliable and the devices do not move.

items.text: Student laptops moving between classrooms.
items.why: Students move around, so mobility matters most.

items.text: A building 800 m from the main school.
items.why: 800 m is far beyond Ethernet's 100 m limit.

items.text: A teacher's tablet in the staff room.
items.why: A mobile device with no need for a cable.

blocks.title: The farm shed
blocks.intro: A farm has a house and a machinery shed 400 m apart. The owner wants internet in the shed and on her phone around the house.

steps.situation: The shed is 400 m from the house.
steps.prompt: Which medium should connect the shed to the house?

choices.text: Optic fibre, because 400 m is beyond Ethernet's 100 m limit and fibre is very fast with no interference.
choices.feedback: It picks a medium and justifies it with distance and speed.

choices.text: Wired Ethernet, because it is cheap.
choices.feedback: Ethernet only reaches about 100 m, so it will not work at 400 m.

choices.text: Wi-Fi from the house, because it needs no cable.
choices.feedback: Wireless reaches tens of metres, and walls and distance weaken it.

steps.situation: She wants to use her phone around the house.
steps.prompt: Which medium suits her phone inside the house?

choices.text: Wireless, because the phone moves around and needs no cable.
choices.feedback: Mobility is wireless's main strength.

choices.text: Optic fibre to the phone.
choices.feedback: A phone cannot plug into fibre as it moves around.

choices.text: Wired Ethernet to the phone.
choices.feedback: A cable would stop the phone being mobile.

blocks.heading: Sparky's rule
blocks.text: Distance and obstacles are the two things that kill wireless every time, and clients never think about either until it has already failed. For anything outdoors or through brick, I default to recommending a wired run, even when it is a harder sell.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Compare wired and wireless media for a home office. (4 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark: "Wireless is easier."
cards.text: One side, no feature.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "Wired Ethernet is faster and more reliable for the desktop because walls do not affect it, but wireless lets the laptop move around the house without cables." Both sides, on named features.

cards.heading: Scenario: The farm

question.text: Recommend a transmission medium to connect the shed to the house, and justify it.
question.explanation: 3 marks – Recommends optic fibre (1) and justifies with two reasons (400 m is beyond Ethernet's 100 m limit; high speed; no interference) (2)

question.text: Compare wired and wireless media for devices inside the house.
question.explanation:
4 marks – Compares both on two features linked to the house
2 to 3 marks – One feature compared, or two with no link
1 mark – Describes one medium

cards.heading: Justify with distance
cards.text: Tie the medium to the distance in the scenario: fibre for kilometres, Ethernet to about 100 m.

cards.heading: Compare both sides
cards.text: Two features, both media, each linked to the setting.

cards.text: At least 5/7 on the practice questions. If not, reread the key terms and test tip.

blocks.heading: 🔧 JOB TICKET
blocks.text: A client on a 100/20 plan keeps asking why their evening live stream keeps freezing when their speed test says 100. Transmission rate, upload versus download, and bandwidth explain exactly why a fast-looking plan can still choke — and it's rarely the plan's fault alone.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

cards.heading: Explain the concept of transmission rate.
Convert between units: bps, Mbps, Gbps.
Explain how upload and download rates affect a task.

blocks.title: Download vs upload speed
blocks.brief: A short clip running a speed test and then sending a large file to show why upload is usually the slower number. Suggested source: a teacher-filmed screen recording of a speed test, or a short NBN plans explainer.
watchFor: Why upload matters for live streams
How shared bandwidth slows each device

items.definition: The amount of data sent per second, measured in bits per second (bps).
1 Mbps = 1 million bits per second; 1 Gbps = 1000 Mbps. Note: 8 bits = 1 byte, so 100 Mbps is about 12.5 MB per second.
Speed of data coming to your device, e.g. streaming, downloading.
Speed of data leaving your device, e.g. sending files, video calls. Home plans usually upload much slower than they download.
The maximum rate a connection can carry; shared by every device using it.

blocks.alt: Two pipes of equal length: download carries many data dots per second, upload carries few.

blocks.title: Put the calculation in order
blocks.instruction: Tap the four steps for working out how long a transfer takes.
items: Find the size in bytes, e.g. 2 GB = 2000 MB.
Convert to bits by multiplying by 8: 2000 MB x 8 = 16 000 megabits.
Divide by the rate: 16 000 / 20 Mbps = 800 s.
Convert to a sensible unit: 800 s is about 13 minutes.
blocks.explanation: Bytes to bits, then divide by the rate. Bits are not bytes, so skipping the x 8 gives an answer eight times too small.

question.text: How long does a 500 MB file take to upload at 40 Mbps?
question.explanation: 500 MB x 8 = 4000 megabits. 4000 / 40 Mbps = 100 seconds.

blocks.title: Check your understanding
blocks.instruction: Answer first, then flip.

cards.front: How many Mbps in 1 Gbps? How many bits in a byte?
cards.back: 1 Gbps = 1000 Mbps. 8 bits = 1 byte.

cards.front: What does a 100/20 plan mean?
cards.back: 100 Mbps download and 20 Mbps upload. Upload is usually much slower.

cards.front: Why does the evening stream freeze when the family is online too?
cards.back: Bandwidth is shared by every device, so less is left for the stream, and upload is already the lower number.

cards.front: Which number limits a live video stream?
cards.back: The upload rate, because the stream is data leaving your device.

blocks.title: The freezing live stream
blocks.intro: A gamer in Bunbury has a 50/20 Mbps plan. He live-streams every evening while his family streams TV and videos.

steps.situation: His speed test says 50 Mbps but the stream freezes.

choices.text: The connection's bandwidth is shared with the family's streaming, and his stream depends on the 20 Mbps upload rate, which is much lower than the download.
choices.feedback: It names shared bandwidth and the upload ceiling.

choices.text: The internet is slow.
choices.feedback: Too vague. It does not name a cause.

choices.text: He needs a faster download plan.
choices.feedback: A live stream depends on upload, so faster download alone would not help.

steps.situation: He wants a solution.

choices.text: Move to a plan with a higher upload rate, or stream when the family is not using the connection.
choices.feedback: It targets upload or the shared bandwidth.

choices.text: Buy a bigger TV.
choices.feedback: Unrelated to the transmission rate.

choices.text: Restart the game.
choices.feedback: The problem is the connection's capacity, not the game.

blocks.heading: Sparky's warning
blocks.text: Download and upload rates are almost never the same number, and a live stream depends on upload, the number everyone forgets to check. If you are uploading video, the 20 is your real ceiling, not the headline 100.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Explain how the upload rate affects sending a large video. (2 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark: "It will be slow."
cards.text: No link to the rate or the task.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "The upload rate is only 20 Mbps, so a 2 GB video takes about 13 minutes to send; a faster upload rate would reduce this time." The rate, the task and the effect.

cards.heading: Scenario: The evening streamer
cards.text: A gamer in Bunbury has a 50/20 Mbps plan. He live-streams his games every evening while his family streams TV and videos. Answer the questions below using this scenario.

question.text: Explain the concept of transmission rate.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Explains the amount of data sent per second, measured in bits per second (e.g. Mbps)
1 mark – States it is internet speed

question.text: Explain why his live stream keeps freezing in the evening, and suggest one solution.
question.explanation:
3 marks – Explains the connection's bandwidth is shared with family streaming, so less is available for his stream, and the 20 Mbps upload rate is already much lower than download
1 mark – Suggests a relevant solution (e.g. a wired connection, lower stream quality, or a plan with a higher upload rate)

cards.heading: Bits are not bytes
cards.text: Multiply bytes by 8, then divide by the rate in Mbps.

cards.heading: Name upload and shared bandwidth
cards.text: Do not just say 'slow internet'.

cards.heading: Aim for
cards.text: At least 5/6 on the practice questions. If not, reread the key terms and test tip.

blocks.heading: 🔧 JOB TICKET
blocks.text: A client asked me, completely seriously, whether their router and their modem were the same box with two names. They're not, and knowing the difference — modem, router, switch, NIC, server — is the difference between diagnosing a fault in five minutes or an hour.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

cards.heading: Describe the purpose of a modem, router, switch, NIC and server.
Explain how data moves between the components.
Identify the components needed for a network.

blocks.title: Inside a home network
blocks.brief: A short clip tracing a photo from a laptop to the internet, naming each device it passes through. Suggested source: a teacher-filmed walk-through of the school's network cabinet, or a home-networking explainer.
watchFor: Why a modem and router are different devices

items.definition: Converts the signal from the service provider's line (e.g. NBN) into data the network can use, and back. For NBN fibre this is often the NBN connection box.
Directs data between the local network and the internet, and gives each device an address. Home routers often include wireless and a switch.
Connects wired devices in a LAN and sends data only to the device it is meant for.
Hardware inside each device that connects it to the network, wired (Ethernet port) or wireless (Wi-Fi).
A computer that provides services to other devices, e.g. storing shared files or running email.

blocks.title: Put the route in order
blocks.instruction: Tap the devices in the order the photo passes through them.
items: Laptop NIC sends the photo.
Switch links the wired devices in the LAN.
Router directs the data towards the internet.
Modem converts it for the provider's line.
The social media company's servers receive it.
blocks.explanation: NIC, switch, router, modem, internet. A small home router often includes the switch and wireless access.

blocks.title: Name the device from its job
blocks.instruction: Tap the device that does each job.

items.text: Converts the provider's signal so the network can reach the internet.
Directs data between the LAN and the internet and gives devices addresses.
Connects wired devices in a LAN and sends data only to the device it is for.
Hardware inside a computer that connects it to the network.
items.why: That is the network interface card.

items.text: Stores shared files or runs email for other devices.
items.why: A server provides services to other devices.

blocks.title: Check your understanding
blocks.instruction: Answer first, then flip.

cards.front: What is the difference between a modem and a router?
cards.back: The modem connects you to your service provider. The router connects your devices to each other and shares that one connection.

cards.front: Why does every computer need a NIC?
cards.back: It is the hardware that physically connects the computer to the network, wired or wireless. Without it the computer cannot send or receive network data.

cards.front: What is a switch NOT for?
cards.back: Connecting to the internet. That is the router and modem.

blocks.heading: Sparky's tip
blocks.text: Modem connects you to your ISP. Router connects your devices to each other and shares that one internet connection. Mix those up and the marker reads it as not understanding either device, even if the rest of your answer is fine.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Describe the purpose of a switch. (2 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark: "It connects to the internet."
cards.text: That is the router and modem.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "A switch connects the wired devices within the LAN and sends data only to the device it is addressed to." The right job and how it works.

cards.heading: Scenario: The design studio
cards.text: A small design studio has three wired desktop computers, a network printer, a file server and staff laptops that use Wi-Fi. Answer the questions below using this scenario.

question.text: Describe the purpose of the router and the modem in the studio's network.
Explain why each computer needs a NIC.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Explains the NIC is the hardware that physically connects the computer to the network (wired or wireless); without it the computer cannot send or receive network data
1 mark – States it connects the computer

cards.heading: Separate router and modem
cards.text: Never blend their roles into one description.

cards.heading: Explain the NIC
cards.text: It is the hardware that connects a device to the network.

cards.heading: Aim for
cards.text: At least 5/6 on the practice questions. If not, reread the key terms and test tip.

blocks.heading: 🔧 JOB TICKET
blocks.text: Two jobs on my desk this week, same question: wired star or peer-to-peer, client-server or not. The right topology depends entirely on the client's situation — a physio clinic's needs aren't a home network's needs — and that's exactly what an assessment answer should justify, not just define.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

cards.heading: Describe wired star and wireless topologies.
Select a topology for a given situation.

blocks.title: Network layouts compared
blocks.brief: A short clip comparing a small peer-to-peer home network with a client-server office, and a wired star with a wireless setup. Suggested source: a teacher-filmed comparison or a networking basics explainer.
watchFor: How devices are connected in a star
Where files are stored in each model

items.definition: The layout of how devices are connected in a network.
Every device connects by cable to a central switch. If one cable fails, only that device is affected; if the switch fails, all are.
Devices connect by radio waves to a wireless access point or router.
A central server stores files and controls access; clients request services from it.
All devices are equal and share directly with each other; no central server.

blocks.explanation: The layout of a network is called its topology.

blocks.title: Client-server or peer-to-peer?
blocks.instruction: Which model does each statement describe?

items.text: A central server stores records and controls who can see what.
items.why: Central control is a client-server feature.

items.text: Devices share files and printers directly with each other.
items.why: There is no central server in peer-to-peer.

items.text: Backed up centrally every night.
items.why: Central backup is a client-server advantage.

items.text: Cheap and simple to set up for a four-person household.
items.why: Low cost and simple suits homes and very small offices.

items.text: Needs more expertise and costs more upfront.
items.why: A server and an administrator add cost and skill.

items.text: Security is set on each device separately.
items.why: There is no central access control.

blocks.title: The physiotherapy clinic
blocks.intro: A physiotherapy clinic with eight staff stores patient records that must be secure and backed up daily.

steps.situation: The clinic must choose a network model.

choices.text: Client-server: central security, daily central backup and controlled access to records.
choices.feedback: It picks a side and justifies it with the clinic's needs.

choices.text: Peer-to-peer, because it is cheaper.
choices.feedback: Cost alone ignores the clinic's security and backup needs.

choices.text: Either, they are both fine.
choices.feedback: 'Justify' means pick a side and defend it.

blocks.heading: Sparky's rule
blocks.text: Client-server costs more upfront but centralises control and backups, so it is worth it the moment multiple people need shared, managed access to the same data. Peer-to-peer is cheap and simple but falls apart past a handful of devices. Match the answer to the scale of the business.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Justify a peer-to-peer network for the household. (3 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark: "It is good for homes."
cards.text: No link to this household.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "With only four people and a few devices, they can share the printer and photos directly without buying a server or needing an administrator, keeping costs low." Reasons tied to the household.

question.text: Describe a wired star topology.

question.text: Justify whether the clinic should use a client-server or peer-to-peer network.
question.explanation:
4 marks – Identifies client-server (1) and justifies with three points linked to the clinic (central security, daily central backup, controlled access to records) (3)
2 to 3 marks – Identifies with one or two linked reasons
1 mark – Identifies only

cards.heading: Describe the star
cards.text: Every device has its own cable to a central switch.

blocks.heading: 🔧 JOB TICKET
blocks.text: The Nguyen family wants their whole house networked and I've got one shot to get the router placement and wiring right before the drywall goes back up. This is the practical end of everything we've covered — floor plan, wireless coverage, and where a wired connection genuinely beats wireless.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

cards.heading: Place network components in suitable locations on a floor plan.
Label each connection as wired or wireless and name the transmission media.
Justify design choices using the scenario.

blocks.title: Designing a home network
blocks.brief: A short clip walking through a home floor plan: placing the router, deciding what to cable and what to leave wireless, and annotating the plan. Suggested source: a teacher-filmed whiteboard walk-through using the Nguyen floor plan.
watchFor: Where the connection enters the house
How coverage is checked room by room

items.definition: Drawing the network on a plan of the building to show where each device and connection goes.
The area the Wi-Fi signal reaches. Walls and distance weaken it; a second access point or mesh unit extends it.
A label naming the device or connection and why it is placed there.

blocks.title: The design checklist
blocks.instruction: Tap the four design steps in order.
items: Entry point: start at the NBN point and place the modem and router.
Wired devices: cable fixed, high-use devices, adding a switch if needed.
Wireless: check every room is covered, adding an access point or mesh unit.
Annotate: label every device, connection (wired or wireless) and medium.
blocks.explanation: Entry point, wired, wireless, annotate. Every placement needs a reason, not just a dot.

spots.label: Upstairs hallway, central to the bedrooms and office

devices.name: Modem and router
devices.why: Place them at the NBN point in the garage, where the optic fibre from the street enters the house.

devices.name: Extra wireless access point (to cover upstairs)
devices.why: The upstairs hallway is central, so the signal reaches the office and bedrooms through fewer walls and the floor.

devices.name: Ethernet connection for the home office desktop
devices.why: A wired run to the desk gives a reliable, fast connection for video calls and large uploads that does not drop upstairs.

devices.name: Shared network printer
devices.why: It sits where it is used in the home office, and joins the network wirelessly so every device can print.

blocks.title: Check your understanding
blocks.instruction: Answer first, then flip.

cards.front: What must every connection on the plan show?
cards.back: Whether it is wired or wireless, and the medium, such as 'wired (Ethernet)' or 'optic fibre'.

cards.front: Why give the home office desktop a wired connection?
cards.back: Wired is faster and more reliable, so video calls and uploads do not drop, and signal is not lost through the floor.

cards.front: Why add a wireless access point or mesh unit upstairs?
cards.back: Walls and distance weaken the signal, so a second unit extends coverage to the far rooms.

blocks.heading: Sparky's rule
blocks.text: I put the router as close to the centre of the house as the internet entry point allows, not wherever is convenient to hide the box. Coverage dies in corners. And anything that needs a rock-solid connection, like a home office desktop on video calls, gets a wired run even in an otherwise wireless house.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Complete the home network design on the floor plan. (8 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark: Lines drawn with no labels.
cards.text: The marker cannot tell wired from wireless, or which box is the router.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: Every device named, every connection labelled wired (Ethernet) or wireless, optic fibre shown from the street, and a short reason next to the router and access point.

cards.heading: Scenario: The two-storey home
cards.text: A two-storey home: NBN point in the downstairs garage; home office upstairs with a desktop and printer; teenagers' bedrooms upstairs with laptops; lounge downstairs with a smart TV. Answer the questions below using this scenario.

question.text: Describe where you would place the router and one other network device, with a reason for each.
Justify a wired connection for the home office desktop.
question.explanation:
3 marks – Justifies with two or more reasons linked to the office (reliable connection for work video calls, faster file uploads, no loss of signal upstairs)
2 marks – One linked reason
1 mark – States wired is faster

cards.heading: Justify placement
cards.text: Each device needs a reason tied to coverage or the entry point.

cards.heading: Annotate everything
cards.text: Label every device, wired or wireless, and the medium.

cards.heading: Aim for
cards.text: At least 5/7 on the practice questions. If not, reread the key terms and test tip.

blocks.heading: 📋 CASE FILE
blocks.text: A ticket seller wants to collect a buyer's school as part of signup and asked me if that's even allowed. Under the Privacy Act 1988 — collection, use, access — the answer is almost never a flat yes or no, it's 'only if it's necessary for the purpose', and most businesses over-collect without realising it.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

cards.heading: State the role of the Privacy Act 1988.
Describe rules for collecting and using personal information.
Describe a person's right to access their information.

blocks.title: The Privacy Act in plain English
blocks.brief: A short explainer on what personal information is and the basic rules for collecting, using and accessing it. Suggested source: the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) education material, or a teacher-filmed screen recording.
watchFor: The 'only collect what you need' rule
How a person asks to see their information

items.definition: Australian law that regulates how government agencies and most organisations (generally those with turnover over $3 million, plus some smaller ones such as health providers) handle personal information, through the Australian Privacy Principles.
Information that identifies a person or could reasonably identify them: name, address, date of birth, photo, phone number.
Only collect information that is needed, and tell people why it is collected and how it will be used (privacy policy).
Use information for the purpose it was collected for, unless the person agrees or the law allows.
People can ask to see the personal information held about them and ask for it to be corrected.

blocks.title: Put the life cycle in order
blocks.instruction: Tap the five stages in order, starting with the first.
items: Collect only what is needed, and say why.
Use it for the stated purpose.
Store it securely.
Let people access and correct it.
Dispose of it when it is no longer needed.
blocks.explanation: Collect, use, store, access, dispose. The rules apply at every stage, not just when data is first collected.

blocks.text: Gym app: OK or not OK?

blocks.title: Sort the gym chain's actions
blocks.instruction: A national gym chain handles its members' details. Is each action OK or not OK under the Privacy Act?

items.text: Collecting name, email, payment details and an emergency contact to run the membership.
items.why: Each item is needed to run the membership.

items.text: Asking new members for their religion and income.
items.why: Not needed for a gym membership, so it should not be collected.

items.text: Sending class reminders to members who signed up.
items.why: It uses the information for the purpose it was collected for.

items.text: Selling member emails to a supplement company without consent.
items.why: It uses the information for a different purpose without agreement.

items.text: Letting a member see a copy of her data and correct her old address.
items.why: People have a right to access and correct information held about them.

blocks.title: Four ideas to lock in
blocks.instruction: Answer first, then flip.

cards.front: What does the Privacy Act 1988 do?
cards.back: It regulates how government agencies and most organisations handle personal information, through the Australian Privacy Principles.

cards.front: What is the collection rule?
cards.back: Only collect information that is needed, and tell people why it is collected and how it will be used.

cards.front: When can information be used for a different purpose?
cards.back: Only if the person agrees or the law allows it.

cards.front: What is the access right?
cards.back: People can ask to see the personal information held about them and ask for incorrect details to be corrected.

blocks.title: The concert ticket seller
blocks.intro: A large online ticket seller's signup form asks for name, email, phone, date of birth and the buyer's school. Rule on it.

steps.situation: The form asks for the buyer's school name to sell a concert ticket.

choices.text: No. It is not needed to sell a ticket, so only necessary information should be collected.
choices.feedback: Collection must be necessary for the purpose. A ticket sale does not need a school name.

choices.text: Yes, because the customer is free to leave it blank.
choices.feedback: Making it optional does not fix over-collection. The test is whether it is necessary.

choices.text: Yes, because more data is always useful.
choices.feedback: Collecting more than needed is exactly what the Act discourages.

steps.situation: A customer emails asking what the seller holds about her and says her phone number is out of date.

choices.text: Let her see her information and correct the phone number.
choices.feedback: People have the right to access their information and have incorrect details corrected.

choices.text: Refuse, because the data belongs to the company.
choices.feedback: The person has a right to access personal information about them.

choices.text: Delete her whole account without telling her.
choices.feedback: That does not answer her request to see or correct her information.

blocks.heading: Elara's test
blocks.text: For every collection question ask: is this piece of personal information actually necessary for what it is being used for? A gym app needs your name and payment details. It very rarely needs your school. If it is not necessary, collecting it is the problem, even if the person consented.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Describe one requirement of the Privacy Act 1988 when collecting information. (2 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark: "They need a good reason."
cards.text: Too vague, with no link to the Act's rules.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "The organisation must only collect information it needs, and must tell the person why it is collected and how it will be used." A specific rule, stated fully.

cards.heading: Scenario: Online ticket seller
cards.text: A large online ticket seller asks for name, email, phone, date of birth and the name of the buyer's school when selling concert tickets. Answer the questions below using this scenario.

question.text: Explain whether the ticket seller should collect the school name.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Explains it should not, because it is not needed to sell a ticket; only necessary information should be collected
1 mark – States no, with no reason

question.text: Describe the right a customer has to access their personal information.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Describes the right to ask to see the information held and to have incorrect details corrected
1 mark – States they can see their information

cards.heading: Use the necessity test
cards.text: Explain collection against 'is it needed?', not just yes or no.

cards.heading: Name the access right
cards.text: People can see the information held about them and have errors corrected.

cards.heading: Aim for
cards.text: At least 3/4 on the practice questions. If not, reread the key terms and test tip.

blocks.heading: 📋 CASE FILE
blocks.text: A clinic is replacing its computers and asked me whether they can just put the old ones out for e-waste collection. The answer involves identity theft risk, what counts as a notifiable data breach, and safe disposal — and getting this wrong isn't just an IT mistake, it's a legal one.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

cards.heading: Describe how identity theft can occur.
Explain the organisation's responsibility to protect and dispose of data.

blocks.title: From data breach to identity theft
blocks.brief: A short clip showing how stolen details are used to open accounts in someone else's name, and what safe disposal of old devices looks like. Suggested source: the Scamwatch or IDCARE education material, or a teacher-filmed screen recording.
watchFor: Which details are most useful to a thief
Why deleted files can still be recovered
What a data-wipe or shredding service does

items.definition: Using someone's personal information to pretend to be them, e.g. to open accounts, take loans or make purchases.
Personal information is lost or accessed without permission, e.g. through hacking.
Under the Privacy Act, organisations must tell affected people and the regulator when a breach is likely to cause serious harm.
Destroying or de-identifying personal information when it is no longer needed, so it cannot be recovered.

blocks.title: How a breach becomes identity theft
blocks.alt: Data held by a company is stolen in a breach and then used to commit identity theft.

cards.heading: How it happens
cards.text: Data breach at a company. Phishing emails and fake websites. Oversharing online (birthday, address, pet names). Stolen mail or recovered old drives.

cards.heading: Reduce the risk
cards.text: Share only what is needed. Strong, unique passwords and two-step verification. Check bank statements. Securely dispose of old devices and documents.

blocks.title: Safe or unsafe disposal?
blocks.instruction: A medical clinic is getting rid of five old computers and paper records. Is each method safe or unsafe?

items.text: Deleting the files and putting the computers in a skip.
items.why: Deleted files can be recovered with free tools.

items.text: Using data-wiping software that overwrites the whole drive.
items.why: Overwriting the whole drive means the old records cannot be recovered.

items.text: Removing the drives and having a certified service shred them.
items.why: Physical destruction makes the data unrecoverable.

items.text: Putting printed patient records in the recycling bin.
items.why: Paper records must be shredded, not recycled whole.

items.text: Emptying the recycle bin on every computer before donating them.
items.why: Emptying the recycle bin does not erase the data from the drive.

blocks.title: Match the term to its definition
blocks.instruction: Tap a term on the left, then tap its definition.

right: Using someone's personal information to pretend to be them, e.g. to open accounts, take loans or make purchases.
Personal information is lost or accessed without permission, e.g. through hacking.
Under the Privacy Act, organisations must tell affected people and the regulator when a breach is likely to cause serious harm.
Destroying or de-identifying personal information when it is no longer needed, so it cannot be recovered.

links: Using someone's personal information to pretend to be them, e.g. to open accounts, take loans or make purchases.
Personal information is lost or accessed without permission, e.g. through hacking.
Under the Privacy Act, organisations must tell affected people and the regulator when a breach is likely to cause serious harm.
Destroying or de-identifying personal information when it is no longer needed, so it cannot be recovered.

blocks.explanation: Identity theft and data breaches are related but distinct — knowing which obligation applies starts with naming the right term.

blocks.title: Check your understanding
blocks.instruction: Answer first, then flip.

cards.front: What is a notifiable data breach?
cards.back: A breach likely to cause serious harm. The organisation must tell the affected people and the regulator.

cards.front: Why is 'delete' not safe disposal?
cards.back: Deleted files can be recovered. Safe disposal means wiping by overwriting the whole drive, or destroying it.

cards.front: Name two ways to reduce your own identity theft risk.
cards.back: Any two of: share only what is needed, use strong unique passwords with two-step verification, check bank statements, dispose of old devices and documents securely.

blocks.heading: Elara's distinction
blocks.text: A data breach only becomes notifiable under the Act when it is likely to cause serious harm. Not every leak triggers the same obligations. Knowing that distinction separates a business that overreacts to every incident from one that correctly escalates the serious ones.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Describe one method of safe disposal. (2 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark: "Delete the files and empty the recycle bin."
cards.text: The data can still be recovered. Earns 0.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "Use data-wiping software to overwrite the entire drive several times, so the old records cannot be recovered." A named method and why it works.

cards.heading: Scenario: Retail chain breach
cards.text: A retail chain's customer database, including names, addresses, dates of birth and driver's licence numbers, was stolen by hackers. Answer the questions below using this scenario.

question.text: Describe how the stolen data could be used for identity theft.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Describes using the details to pretend to be a customer, e.g. to open a credit card or loan in their name
1 mark – States hackers can use the data

question.text: Explain two responsibilities the retailer has under the Privacy Act 1988 for this data.

cards.heading: Link data to a real misuse
cards.text: Say what a thief does with it, such as opening a credit card or loan in the victim's name.

cards.heading: Delete is not disposal
cards.text: Name wiping or destruction, and say why the data cannot then be recovered.

cards.heading: Aim for
cards.text: At least 5/6 on the practice questions. If not, reread the key terms and test tip.

blocks.heading: 📋 CASE FILE
blocks.text: A council report crossed my desk arguing a new online-only service would 'improve access for everyone' — it wouldn't, and naming exactly who ends up on the wrong side of the digital divide is the whole point of this case. Availability of resources, ability to use them, and dependency on electronic communication are three separate barriers, not one.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

cards.heading: Explain the concept of the digital divide.
Describe issues: availability of digital resources, dependency on electronic communication, use of digital technologies, availability of web-based applications.
Explain the effect on a person or group.

blocks.title: What is the digital divide?
blocks.brief: A short clip with real examples of people who are left out when services move online, including rural and older Australians. Suggested source: material from the Australian Digital Inclusion Index, or a teacher-filmed example.
watchFor: Who is on each side of the divide
Why a connection alone does not fix it

items.definition: The gap between people who have access to digital technologies and the skills to use them, and people who do not.
Whether people can get devices and a reliable, affordable internet connection.
Whether people have the skills and confidence to use them.
Whether services people need online (banking, government, study) work on their device and connection.
Services moving online-only, which disadvantages people without access.
