blocks.text: Who is on the wrong side?

blocks.title: Which issue is it?
blocks.instruction: Each situation shows one barrier. Tap the issue it best matches.

items.text: A farmer 60 km from town has slow satellite internet, so video calls and uploads often fail.
items.why: A reliable, affordable connection is a digital resource he does not have.

items.text: An 82-year-old has a phone but not the skills to use myGov or online banking.
items.why: The barrier is skills and confidence in using the technology.

items.text: A family on a low income shares one phone with limited data between three school children.
items.why: Not enough devices or data is an availability of resources issue.

items.text: A bank closes its only town branch and tells customers to use its app.
items.why: A service moving online-only disadvantages people without access.

items.text: A government form will not load properly on an older phone with a weak signal.
items.why: The web-based service does not work on the person's device and connection.

blocks.title: Why it matters now
blocks.intro: Services that now mainly run online:

cards.heading: Everyday services
cards.text: Banking and bill payment. Government services such as myGov and Centrelink. Health appointments by telehealth.

cards.heading: Study and work
cards.text: School work and reports. Job applications.

cards.heading: Effects of being left out
cards.text: Missed information and deadlines. Higher costs such as paper bills and travel. Falling behind at school or work.

cards.heading: Social effects
cards.text: Social isolation. Relying on others for private matters.

blocks.title: The branch that closed
blocks.intro: A bank closes its only branch in a small country town and tells customers to use its app. Pick the strongest explanation each time.

steps.situation: Older residents mostly have basic phones and have never used banking apps.
steps.prompt: Which answer best explains the effect on them?

choices.text: They struggle.
choices.feedback: Too vague. It does not say which group or what happens to them.

choices.text: Without app skills they must travel to another town to bank, which costs time and money.
choices.feedback: It names the group, the barrier and the effect.

choices.text: They should just learn to use the app.
choices.feedback: That is advice, not an effect, and it ignores the barrier.

steps.situation: Some farms on the edge of town have slow satellite internet.
steps.prompt: Which answer best explains the effect on them?

choices.text: Slow satellite internet means the app and uploads often fail, so they must drive to a branch in another town, losing a day of work.
choices.feedback: It links the specific barrier to a specific consequence.

choices.text: They have bad internet.
choices.feedback: It states the issue but not the effect.

choices.text: Internet is cheap now so it is fine.
choices.feedback: Not true for rural users, and it avoids the question.

blocks.heading: Elara's warning
blocks.text: People conflate 'has internet access' with 'digital divide solved'. Someone can have a connection and still be excluded if they lack the skills, the right device or the confidence to use a service. The divide is about capability as much as access.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Explain how the digital divide affects the farmer. (3 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark: "He has bad internet."
cards.text: States the issue but not the effect.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "Slow satellite internet means he cannot reliably use telehealth or upload records to government sites, so he must drive to town, losing a day of work." Issue, then a specific effect.

cards.heading: Scenario: The closed bank branch
cards.text: A bank closes its only branch in a small country town and tells customers to use its app. Answer the questions below using this scenario.

question.text: Explain the concept of the digital divide.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Explains the gap between those with access to and skills in digital technologies and those without
1 mark – States some people do not have technology

question.text: Explain how this change could affect two different groups in the town.

cards.heading: Define the gap
cards.text: People with access and skills versus people without.

cards.heading: Name the group
cards.text: Say which people and why, such as older residents without app skills or rural residents without a reliable connection.

cards.heading: Aim for
cards.text: At least 5/6 on the practice questions. If not, reread the key terms and test tip.

blocks.heading: 📋 CASE FILE
blocks.text: A Bunbury surf shop went online this year and the owner's thrilled about 24/7 sales — and surprised by the 2am customer emails expecting instant replies. E-commerce, improved digital communication, round-the-clock trading: every benefit comes with a matched cost, and a strong assessment response should include both.

Describe implications of improved digital communications.
Explain positive and negative implications of 24/7 communication.

items.definition: Buying and selling goods and services over the internet.
Faster internet, mobile devices and apps that let businesses and customers connect instantly.
Customers can shop, message and expect replies at any time of day, every day.
Paying through card, digital wallet or buy now pay later services.

blocks.title: Positive or negative?
blocks.instruction: Sort each implication of 24/7 online trading for a small business.

items.text: Orders arrive at 2 am while the shop is closed.
Customers message on Instagram at night and expect quick replies.
items.why: It creates pressure to reply out of hours, adding workload or cost.

items.text: The shop sells wetsuits to customers across Australia, not only locals.
items.why: A wider reach means more potential customers.

items.text: The owner finds it hard to switch off from the business.
items.why: Round-the-clock contact blurs work and personal time.

items.text: The shop now competes with global online stores on price.
items.why: Customers can compare prices easily, which squeezes margins.

items.text: Chatbots can answer common questions at any hour.
items.why: It helps meet 24/7 expectations without extra staff, though it has a set-up cost.

cards.heading: Positive
cards.text: Shop any time, from anywhere. Compare prices easily.

cards.heading: Negative
cards.text: Cannot see or try products first. Risk of scams and data theft.

blocks.title: Check your understanding
blocks.instruction: Answer first, then flip.

cards.front: What is e-commerce?
cards.back: Buying and selling goods and services over the internet.

cards.front: What does 24/7 communication mean?
cards.back: Customers can shop, message and expect replies at any time of day, every day.

cards.front: Give one positive and one negative of 24/7 trading for a small business.
cards.back: Positive: more sales outside normal hours. Negative: customers expect replies at night, adding workload or cost.

cards.front: What is the most common mistake in a 'positive and negative' answer?
cards.back: Giving two positives dressed up differently. One answer must be a real negative.

blocks.heading: Elara's double edge
blocks.text: 24/7 availability grows sales outside normal hours, and it also creates an expectation of round-the-clock responsiveness that small operators struggle to meet. Always give both sides.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Describe one implication of 24/7 communication for a small business. (2 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark: "It is always open."
cards.text: That is the feature, not the consequence.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "Customers expect replies at night, so the owner must answer messages after hours or pay for a chatbot, adding workload or cost." A consequence for the business.

cards.text: E-commerce is buying and selling goods and services over the internet.

blocks.text: A school's systems went down for a day and it exposed exactly how dependent the staff and even the patients at the attached clinic had become on electronic communication. Explain an issue for a person or organisation.

blocks.instruction: Sort each point under the issue it belongs to.

items.text: Jobs need new software skills every few years.
items.why: People must keep developing their technology skills.

items.text: Screenshots can be shared without permission.
items.why: Users are responsible for what they share and how they protect information.

blocks.title: The medical centre app
blocks.intro: A medical centre moves appointments, reminders and test results to an app, and staff mostly talk to patients by video call.

steps.situation: A patient has to log in to see her test results.
steps.prompt: Which is the strongest privacy responsibility for her?

choices.text: Use a strong password and do not share her login details.
choices.feedback: Protecting her own login is her responsibility, since it controls access to her results.

choices.text: Let a friend log in for her so it is easier.
choices.feedback: Sharing login details gives others access to private health information.

choices.text: Write the password on the back of her phone.
choices.feedback: That makes it easy for someone else to find and use.

steps.situation: She has a video appointment while at a busy cafe.

choices.text: Take the call somewhere private so others cannot see or hear it.
choices.feedback: Video calls can show and expose private details, so choosing a private space is her responsibility.

choices.text: Take it at the cafe table and speak louder.
choices.feedback: Other people could overhear private health details.

choices.text: Screenshot the doctor's screen to post to a group.
choices.feedback: Sharing a screenshot without permission breaches the doctor's and her own privacy.

blocks.title: Check your understanding
blocks.instruction: Answer first, then flip.

cards.front: What is dependency on electronic and visual communication?
cards.back: Relying on tools such as email, messaging and video calls so much that work and daily life cannot happen without them.

cards.front: Why must people keep developing technology skills?
cards.back: New tools keep arriving, and without the skills people cannot take part in work, study and services, or need retraining.

cards.front: What lesson did the school outage teach?
cards.back: Keep offline backups and a plan for outages.

blocks.heading: Elara's view
blocks.text: Dependency is not automatically a flaw to criticise. It is a fact to manage. The useful answer is not 'people should not rely on technology', it is naming the specific skill gap or responsibility that the outage exposed, and what closes it.

blocks.intro: Explain one issue of society's dependency on electronic communication. (3 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark: "People use phones too much."
cards.text: Not linked to an issue in the syllabus.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "Workers need to keep learning new tools, such as a new booking system, so staff without training are left behind or need retraining, which costs the business time." A named issue with a consequence.

1 mark – States a responsibility

cards.heading: Name the skill

cards.text: At least 4/5 on the practice questions. If not, reread the key terms and test tip.

blocks.heading: 🎟️ TICKET
blocks.text: Three students planning the Year 12 formal are scattered across different towns and need to actually get work done together, not just message about it. Choosing the right collaboration tools — and being honest about the real downside — is the difference between a project that moves and one stuck in a group chat forever.

blocks.title: By the end of this lesson you can

cards.heading: Describe how each type supports a team.
Explain advantages and disadvantages of online collaboration.

blocks.title: Working together online
blocks.brief: A short clip showing three students co-authoring a document, chatting in Teams and leaving comments. Suggested source: a teacher-filmed screen recording using school Microsoft 365.
watchFor: Who is editing at the same time

rows: People working together on the same task using internet-based tools.
Several people edit the same file at the same time.
Live meetings with video and audio.
Storing files online so the team can access them.
Feedback attached to parts of a file, and a record of changes.

blocks.title: The group video
blocks.intro: Three students make a group video. One edits, one writes the script, one finds music. They live in different towns.

steps.situation: Which two types of collaboration would suit them?

choices.text: Video conferencing to plan together, and cloud file sharing so the editor always has the latest script and music.

choices.text: Email attachments only.

blocks.title: Set Up a Real Shared Planning Doc
blocks.intro: Set up the kind of shared document the three Year 12 formal planners from this lesson would actually need — then test it with a classmate, not just by yourself.
steps: Create a new document titled Formal Planning — [your name].
Add three headed sections: Budget, Run Sheet, Vendor Contacts.
Share it with a classmate with Editor permission (not just Viewer).
Have your classmate add a comment on one section and make one direct edit elsewhere in the document at the same time as you're editing it.
Check the document's version history (File > Version history) and confirm both sets of changes are visible with timestamps.
Resolve the comment your classmate left.
Write two sentences: one real advantage this showed you, and one real disadvantage (e.g. conflicting edits, needing to agree on structure first).

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: The disadvantage question is the one everyone skips, because collaboration tools feel like an unqualified good. They're not — version confusion, unequal contribution, or someone's patchy wifi dropping them from a call are all real costs, and naming one honestly is worth more than pretending collaboration has no downside.

blocks.title: Build a Three-Page Site With a Shared Stylesheet
blocks.software: Any text editor (e.g. VS Code) and a browser
blocks.intro: Build the exact fix the club website in this lesson needed — a shared .css file — so one colour change updates every page at once.
steps: Create three files: index.html, about.html and contact.html, each with a heading and a short paragraph.
Add a navigation menu to each page with internal hyperlinks between all three pages — test that every link works.
Add one external hyperlink (to a real website) and one email hyperlink (mailto:) somewhere on the site.
Create a single styles.css file and link all three HTML pages to it using <link rel="stylesheet">.
In styles.css, set a background colour and a heading colour.
Change the colour values once, in styles.css only, and reload all three pages to confirm every page updated from one edit.
Write one sentence explaining how long this would have taken if each page had its own separate <style> block instead.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: A .css file is the single highest-leverage thing in basic web authoring — one file controls the look of every page that links to it. Any site that doesn't use one is signing up for exactly the pain this club just went through, and it's completely avoidable.

blocks.title: The zoo guide
blocks.intro: A five-page interactive PDF for a local zoo has Cover, Animals, Opening hours, Map and Contact. Every page links back to the Cover. Animals links to Map.

steps.situation: Identify the structure and justify it.

choices.text: Hierarchical: the Cover is the home page with sections branching from it, so visitors can always get back to the start and jump to what they need.
choices.feedback: It names the structure and links it to the guide's use.

choices.text: Linear, because it has five pages.
choices.feedback: Page count does not make it linear.

choices.text: It has no structure.
choices.feedback: Every product has one.

steps.situation: What must your map show?

choices.text: Only the cover.
choices.feedback: A map shows every page.

choices.text: Colours and fonts.
choices.feedback: That is design, not navigation.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Linear structures suit a fixed sequence a user has to follow — a checkout flow, a tutorial. Hierarchical suits browsing categories, which is exactly what a camping app needs: parks, then sites, then details. Pick the structure the user's actual task demands, not the one that's easiest to diagram.

blocks.title: The cafe website
blocks.intro: A cafe website shows a wide menu table and small buttons. On a phone, customers have to zoom in and scroll sideways.

steps.situation: Which two changes would fix it?

choices.text: Use a fluid layout so the menu stacks into one column on phones, and make the buttons larger so they are easy to tap.
choices.feedback: Two specific responsive changes tied to the problems.

choices.text: Make the site wider.
choices.feedback: That makes scrolling worse.

choices.text: Remove the menu.
choices.feedback: Customers need it.

blocks.title: Make a Page Actually Responsive
blocks.software: Any text editor and a browser
blocks.intro: Take a simple page and deliberately break it on a small screen first, then fix it with real responsive techniques — not by guessing, by testing.
steps: Build a simple HTML page with a header, a navigation menu with 5 links, and a 3-column layout of content using fixed pixel widths (e.g. three divs each width: 400px).
Open your browser's device toolbar (F12 then the device icon, or Ctrl+Shift+M) and switch to a phone-width view.
Note what breaks — likely horizontal scrolling and overlapping columns.
Fix the columns using a fluid, percentage-based or flexbox/grid layout instead of fixed pixel widths.
Add a CSS media query breakpoint that stacks the columns vertically below 600px width.
Replace the 5-link navigation menu with a hamburger menu (a simple toggle button that shows/hides the links) that appears only below the same breakpoint.
Re-test at phone width and confirm there's no horizontal scrolling and the menu toggles correctly.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: A breakpoint isn't a fixed rule you memorise once — it's wherever the current layout actually starts to break for a given screen width, and that's different for every design. Test on the real device, don't guess the number from a textbook.

items.definition: One still image in an animation. Frame rate is frames per second (fps).
A frame where something important changes, such as a start or end position.

blocks.title: Frame by frame or tween?
blocks.instruction: Which method does each description fit?

items.text: Draw the ball in 24 positions for one second at 24 fps.
items.why: Every frame is made by hand.

items.text: Set start and end keyframes and let the software fill the frames between.
Detailed control, such as squash and stretch, but slow to make.
Changing the ball into a star over 12 frames.

blocks.title: Build the title animation
blocks.instruction: Tap the steps in a sensible order.
items: Place the logo off-screen at the start keyframe.
Set the end keyframe with the logo in the centre.
Add a motion tween between the keyframes.
Add a fade-in effect, then a Watch now button that appears at the end.
blocks.explanation: Keyframes first, then the tween, then the button.

blocks.title: The animated title
blocks.intro: A student makes an animated title for a school video: the school logo slides in from the left and fades in, then a Watch now button appears.

steps.situation: How could a tween create the logo movement?

choices.text: Set a start keyframe with the logo off-screen and an end keyframe in the centre, then add a motion tween so the software creates the frames between.
choices.feedback: Keyframes plus tween.

choices.text: Draw all 48 frames by hand.
choices.feedback: That is frame by frame, not a tween.

choices.text: Add a button.
choices.feedback: That does not move the logo.

steps.situation: What is the purpose of the button and its states?

choices.text: A button responds to the user and triggers an action; its up, over and down states show it reacts when idle, hovered and pressed.
choices.feedback: Purpose and states.

choices.text: It makes the animation longer.
choices.feedback: Not its purpose.

choices.text: It sets the frame rate.
choices.feedback: Not its purpose.

blocks.title: Animate a Bouncing Ball With Tweens
blocks.software: Any animation tool with keyframes (e.g. Canva, Adobe Animate, or CSS animation in a browser)
blocks.intro: Build the exact animation from this lesson's worked example — a ball that bounces — using real keyframes and tweening, not a pre-made GIF.
steps: Create a canvas or frame roughly 400×400px with a simple circle as your ball.
Set a keyframe with the ball at the top of the frame.
Set a second keyframe a short time later with the ball at the bottom of the frame.
Apply a tween between the two keyframes and preview it — confirm the software is calculating the frames in between, not that you drew them.
Add a third keyframe that squashes the ball slightly wider and shorter at the moment it hits the bottom, for a more realistic bounce.
Add a simple button (even just a shape) elsewhere in the frame with at least two states — e.g. a different fill colour for 'up' and 'over'.
Export the animation as a GIF or short video.
Write one sentence identifying the start keyframe and end keyframe your tween used.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: A tween isn't magic — it's the software calculating every frame between two keyframes you set manually. If you can't explain that a tween needs a start keyframe and an end keyframe to interpolate between, you don't yet understand why it works, you've just used the button.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Compare frame by frame and tweened animation. (4 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark
cards.text: "Tweening is faster." One side of one feature.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "Tweening is faster because the software creates the in-between frames, while frame by frame is slower but gives full control over every movement."

blocks.instruction: Which of these belong in each row of a plan of action?

items.why: Each task needs a time allocation.

items.text: Resources, such as paper or a laptop.
A favourite colour.
items.why: Not part of a plan of action.

Due date.

items: Interview the band.
Draw wireframes for three pages.

Build the pages.
blocks.explanation: Approval comes before building, because the build depends on it.

blocks.title: The school musical program
blocks.intro: A student has three weeks to design and print a program for the school musical. The drama teacher must approve the design before printing.

steps.situation: Which three tasks, in order, belong in her plan?

choices.text: Design the program (4 hrs, laptop, Canva), teacher approves (milestone), print and check (2 hrs, school printer).
choices.feedback: Ordered, with time and resources, and approval before printing.

choices.text: Print, design, approve.
choices.feedback: Wrong order.

choices.text: Design only.
choices.feedback: A plan lists every task.

blocks.title: Build the Band's Website Plan of Action
blocks.software: Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets, or a word processor table
blocks.intro: Turn the band website brief from this lesson into an actual plan of action with every required part in every row.
steps: Create a table with four columns: Task, Time Estimate, Responsible Person, Dependency.
List at least eight tasks needed to build a simple band website, in a logical order (e.g. 'collect band photos' before 'build the gallery page').
For every task, fill in a realistic time estimate and a responsible person (use fictional names if working alone).
For every task, name its dependency — which earlier task must finish first — or write 'none' if it has no dependency.
Highlight the longest chain of dependent tasks (the critical path) in one colour.
Add one milestone row marking 'Website live' at the end, with its own target date.
Save the file as band-website-plan-of-action.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Dependencies are what separate a task list from a plan. If 'build the gallery page' depends on 'collect band photos' finishing first, and you don't mark that dependency, someone will start the gallery with no photos and waste the sprint. Always ask what has to happen before this.

cards.heading: Earns full marks

blocks.title: The late documentary
blocks.intro: Two students are making a five-minute documentary for a local museum in four weeks. They keep running out of class time and have not started editing.

steps.situation: Which two strategies would help?

choices.text: Set milestones with dates (script, filming, editing) and block fixed time for editing, so progress is checked and editing is not left to the end.
choices.feedback: Two strategies linked to the problem.

choices.text: Work harder.
choices.feedback: Not a strategy.

choices.text: Ask for more time.
choices.feedback: It does not fix the planning.

steps.situation: Why include buffer time?

choices.text: Problems and changes are likely, such as a failed recording, so spare time before the deadline stops one setback making the project late.
choices.feedback: It explains the purpose.

choices.text: So they can finish early and stop.
choices.feedback: Not the purpose.

choices.text: It is not needed.
choices.feedback: Plans without buffer break easily.

blocks.title: Build a Gantt Chart to Rescue a Late Project
blocks.software: Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets, or a dedicated Gantt tool
blocks.intro: Build an actual Gantt chart for the late project from this lesson, with real buffer time included — not just a task list.
steps: List at least six tasks for a simple project of your choice (e.g. producing a short video) down the left column.
Across the top, add column headers for each day or week of the project timeline.
For each task, shade the cells spanning the days it will take, showing tasks that overlap and tasks that depend on earlier ones finishing first.
Add at least one buffer block (a shaded cell explicitly labelled 'Buffer') before the final deadline.
Mark today's date with a vertical line or highlighted column.
Write two sentences: one naming a time management strategy you used building this (prioritising, milestones, time blocking) and one explaining what the buffer protects against.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Buffer time isn't slack for being lazy — it's the only thing standing between 'one task runs long' and 'the whole project misses its deadline'. A plan with zero buffer is a plan that was already late the moment anything went even slightly wrong.

cards.heading: Earns full marks

blocks.title: The walking trails guide
blocks.intro: A student is creating an interactive PDF guide to local walking trails. She needs photos of each trail, InDesign, and feedback from a park ranger.

steps.situation: Identify one hardware, one software and one people resource.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: People are the resource everyone forgets to plan for — hardware and software get listed, but who's editing, who's hosting, who's actually available this week rarely gets the same scrutiny, and it's usually the people resource that causes the delay.

blocks.title: Evaluate the Community Garden Newsletter
blocks.software: Any word processor, plus a survey tool (e.g. Google Forms) if available
blocks.intro: Produce both a product evaluation and a process evaluation for the community garden newsletter from this lesson — two different questions, two different kinds of evidence.
steps: Find or create a simple one-page newsletter (any topic is fine if you don't have a real one).
Write three product evaluation criteria (does the finished newsletter meet the brief — e.g. readable font size, all sections present, fits on one page).
Write two process evaluation questions (did the way the team worked go smoothly — e.g. was the deadline met, did everyone contribute).
Create a short 3-question survey (Google Forms or on paper) asking a reader to rate the newsletter against your product criteria.
Collect at least two responses and summarise the feedback in one paragraph.
Recommend one specific, actionable change for next time's newsletter based on the feedback.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Product evaluation and process evaluation answer different questions — did the final newsletter actually meet the brief, versus did the way the team worked actually go smoothly. A project can nail one and fail the other, and a good evaluation checks both separately.

blocks.title: Test tip: what earns the marks
blocks.intro: Evaluate the product against one design criterion. (3 marks)

cards.heading: Earns 0 or 1 mark
cards.text: "I think it is really good and the client liked it." No criterion, no evidence.

cards.heading: Earns full marks
cards.text: "Criterion: readable on a phone. Partly met: 5 of 12 surveyed members said the text was too small. Increasing body text to 14 pt would fix this."
